<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'I' with stylized floral motifs.</image-desc> I present to you <note>Original: "UE." an abbreviation for "U Edelen," a formal and respectful way of addressing the reader, similar to "Your Honor" or "Your Noble Self."</note> now a small Work, under the title of ALPHABETICAL LIST OF NAMES OF THE Heretics, etc., hoping that the same, because of its brevity, will be received with a favorable hand. ## ABRAHAMITES
, a following of heretics, whom the Arabs call *Ibrahumiah*, after their founder, who bore the name of *Ibrahim*, or *Abraham*. This heretic renewed in Antioch, where he was born, the sect of the *Paulicians* <note>A dualist Christian sect that arose in Armenia in the 7th century</note>, and had already led astray a large part of Syria; when *Cyriacus*, an orthodox Patriarch of this Church, vigorously opposed him, achieving so much that this sect was dispersed. These *Paulicians* recognized as the founder of their group *Paul of Samosata* <note>Paulus Samosetanus, a 3rd-century Bishop of Antioch who was declared a heretic for teaching that Jesus was a man who became divine, rather than God from birth</note>, who denied the divinity of Christ. The Patriarch *Cyriacus*, just mentioned, held the see at Antioch under the reign of *Harun al-Rashid*, Caliph of the *Abbasid* dynasty, around 805 years after Christ's birth. *Nicephorus* was then Emperor in the East, and *Charlemagne* <note>Charles the Great</note> in the West. *Herbelot, Oriental Library.* <note>Referencing the 'Bibliothèque Orientale' by Barthélemy d'Herbelot, a famous 17th-century encyclopedia of Middle Eastern history</note>

Prateolus under the word Abstinents.* <note>Philastrius was a 4th-century bishop; Baronius was a 16th-century Cardinal known for his ecclesiastical history; Prateolus (Gabriel du Préau) was a 16th-century theologian who wrote a catalog of heretics.</note>

**ACEPHALII or ACEPHALANS**, a certain type of Heretics who were named thus because they had no head <note>From the Greek *akephalos*, meaning "headless"</note> over them. Some writers believe they are those who wished to follow neither Patriarch *John* of *Antioch* nor *Cyril* of *Alexandria* in the dispute that existed during the time of *Sixtus III*, after the assembly of the Council of *Ephesus*. However, it is more likely that they arose around the year 482, and that this name was given to those who followed the errors of *Peter Mongus* <note>Also known as "the Stammerer," a 5th-century Patriarch of Alexandria</note>, Bishop of *Alexandria*. The *Acephalans* abandoned him because he appeared to approve the decrees of the Council of *Chalcedon* <note>The Council of 451 AD which defined the dual nature of Christ—truly God and truly man—against the Monophysite view</note>, which they held in abhorrence. Some others say that these Heretics followed the errors of *Severus*, Bishop of *Antioch*, who nevertheless came after them and held a particular view. They refused to tolerate any authority or government, and, alongside *Eutyches* <note>A monk whose teachings led to the Eutychian heresy, claiming Christ’s humanity was absorbed by his divinity</note>, they conflated the two natures of *Christ*, and for this reason were condemned by the Council of *Chalcedon* in the 5th century. *Liberatus in his brief, Chapter 9. Leontius on the Sects, Act 5. Baronius.*

<header>AD of the Heretics.</header>

*Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century bishop of Salamis and author of the *Panarion*, a famous treatise against heresies</note> relates that this name was given to the *Manichean* Heretics of *Mesopotamia*, on account of a certain *Acovana*, a disciple of *Manes* <note>The founder of Manichaeism, a religion that taught a dualistic struggle between light and darkness</note>, who spread his errors in that land.

## ADAMITES

*ADAMITES*, *Epiphanius*, *Augustine*, and subsequently *Theodoret* make mention of a sect of infamous Heretics whom they call *Adamites*. It is believed that this sect was an offshoot of the *Basilidians* and the *Carpocratians* <note>Followers of Basilides and Carpocrates, 2nd-century Gnostic teachers in Alexandria</note>. For *Irenaeus*, in the 1st Chapter of his 1st Book, *Against Heresies* <note>original: "Adversus Haereses"</note> says,

> “that some, based on the principles of the teachings of *Basilides* and of *Carpocrates*, permitted an infamous social intercourse with all sorts of persons, the multiplication of marriages, and the freedom to eat meat that had been offered in sacrifice to the gods of the heathens.” 

But these errors are not exactly the same as those attributed to the *Adamites*. *Theodoret* identifies *Prodicus* as the founder of the *Adamites*. Mention is made of this *Prodicus* by *Tertullian* and by *Clement of Alexandria*; and the latter accuses his disciples of giving themselves every freedom to commit adultery in secret, and to give themselves over to all kinds of lusts. He also notes that they judged prayer to be unnecessary. *Clement of Alexandria* in his 3rd and 7th Books. *Tertullian* places him, alongside *Valentinus* <note>A prominent Gnostic theologian</note>, in the number of Heretics who denied the unity of a single God, and rejected the necessity of the suffering <note>referring to the Passion or physical suffering of Christ</note>. *Tertullian, Against Praxeas, chapter 3.* <note>original: "Tertull. contra Praxem. c. 3."</note>

The impieties that he attributes to them are that they held their meetings in a heated room <note>original: "Kagchel"; likely referring to a hypocaust or a bathhouse-style heated room</note>, and that they, both men and women, entered it naked; that they sat there among one another, and in that state read and performed their prayers. They nevertheless boasted of the gift of abstinence <note>original: "onthouding"; the practice of self-restraint, particularly in regard to sexual relations</note>, and asserted that if anyone fell into sin, they would cast him out of their assembly, just as *Adam* was driven out of the earthly *Paradise* because he had eaten of the forbidden fruit; they regarded themselves as *Adam* and *Eve*, and their temple as *Paradise*. For which reason they are also named *Adamites*. They taught that *Jesus Christ*, with respect to his Divine Nature, was the true and proper Son of God, but that with respect to his human nature, he was nothing other than [the Son] through adoption (*Adoptio*) <note>The theological concept that Jesus was the Son of God by grace or "adoption" in his humanity, rather than being the natural Son of God in both natures</note> and grace. **ADRIANISTS**, thus certain Heretics are named by *Theodoretus* <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD), an influential theologian and church historian</note>, who places them among the number of Heretics who sprang from the Sect of *Simon Magus* (a) <note>original: "Simon den Tovenaar." **ÆSCHINES**, a Heretic, being devoted to the errors of *Montanus* <note>Founder of the Montanist movement, which focused on new prophetic revelations and strict asceticism</note>, whose followers distinguished themselves from other *Montanists* in that they taught that *Christ* was both the Father and the Son in the *Holy Trinity*. *Epiphanius & Philostorgius, On Heresies; appendix to Tertullian, On the Prescription of Heretics, Chapter 52.*

### ETHNOPHRONES, ETHNOPHRONEN, or PAGANISANS,
were Heretics in the 7th century, who indeed presented themselves as Christians, but followed the customs of the Pagans, and practiced fortune-telling, sorcery, and other follies. *John of Damascus <note>original: "Joh. Damasc." A Syrian monk and influential theologian (c. 675–749 AD)</note>; Sanders, Heresies 226; Gualtieri in Chronology.*

### AETIANS
were Heretics and followers of *Arius* <note>The priest from Alexandria whose teachings on the nature of Christ led to the Arian controversy</note> and *Aëtius*, called the *Atheist*, or *Denier of God*. They made up the faction that was called the pure *Arians*, and their error was embraced by *Eunomius*, the principal disciple of *Aëtius*; by *Eudoxius*; by *Acacius of Caesarea*; by *George of Alexandria*, and by most *Western Arians*. They were also called *Eunomians*, or *Anomeans*, after the disciple *Eunomius*. And because they taught that the Son not only had a different Essence than the Father, but was unlike him in everything <note>original Greek: "κατὰ παντα ἀνόμοιον" (kata panta anomoion)</note>, they were also named *Anomii*, *Anomæi*, and *Anomiani* <note>These terms all derive from the Greek word for "unlike" or "dissimilar"</note>. *Theodosius the Great* † drove them out of all his cities; for which reason they stayed here and there in the wildernesses, and came together in secret in private houses, for which reason they were also called *Troglodytes* <note>From the Greek for "cave-dwellers," a name given to them because they were forced to meet in hidden or subterranean places</note>. *Sozomen, Book 7, Chapter 26; Theodoret, Book 4, Heretical Fables.*

**AGNOITANS**, or **AGNOETES**, a sect of Heretics in the 4th century, who followed the errors of *Theophronius of Cappadocia*, who claimed that the knowledge by which God foresees future things, knows the present, and remembers the past, is not the same; which he attempted to prove through some passages from the Holy Scripture. The *Eunomians* <note>An extreme Arian sect that believed the Son was of a different nature than the Father</note>, being unable to tolerate this Teaching, expelled him from their community, and he established himself as the head of a Sect, to which the name *Eunomiophronians* was also given. They also changed the *Baptism*, no longer baptizing in the name of the Holy Trinity, but in the name of the death of *Jesus Christ*. This *Theophronius* had written a Book on the exercise of the spirit, in which he asserted his new opinions, for which he was driven out by the *Eunomians*. It was around the year 370, under the reign of *Valens* <note>Eastern Roman Emperor from 364 to 378 AD</note>, when *Theophronius* became the head of a particular sect. *Socrates, Book 5, Chapter 24; Sozomen, Book 6, Chapter 26, & Book 7, Chapter 27; Nicephorus, Book 12, Chapter 30; Prateolus under the word Agnoites.*

### ALBIGENSES,
commonly called ALBIGOTTES in their time. It is the unanimous opinion of both Roman Catholic and Protestant writers that the ALBIGENSES were a group of people who, in the 12th and the two following centuries, heavily opposed the Roman Church in both doctrine and ceremonies, and especially regarding the supremacy of the Pope and the authority of their Church; and that they were therefore also condemned by that Church as heretics, and persecuted with fire and sword <note>A reference to the Albigensian Crusade and the Inquisition</note>. They were called ALBIGENSES after the very ancient city of Albi, located in France, in the province of Languedoc on the river Tarn, where they first revealed themselves and held their primary residence, and from where they then spread through all of Provence, Languedoc, Bearn, and other surrounding lands—indeed, even subsequently across all of Europe. But as to what their specific beliefs were, besides those in which they opposed the Roman Church, there is no agreement.

Several writers of the Roman Church, and among them primarily *Bossuet* <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704), a prominent French bishop and theologian</note>, first Bishop of Condom and thereafter of Meaux, are of the opinion that the ALBIGENSES held the beliefs of the *Manichaeans* <note>A dualistic religion that saw the world as a struggle between good/spirit and evil/matter</note>, brought over to them from Bulgaria, and those of the *Arians* <note>Those who denied the full divinity of Christ</note>, and also that their way of life...

He was asked whether *Baptism*, administered by a *Priest* who says, "I baptize you," etc., effects the forgiveness of sins? He answered,

### ...of the Heretics.

...the, one can conclude from what has already been reported, that they were pure and godly in their conduct, through which their esteem and following increased, while that of the Priests fell; this is sufficiently evident from the cited testimony of *Guill. de Puy Laurent* <note>Guillaume de Puylaurens (c. 1200–1275), a chronicler who wrote about the Albigensian Crusade</note>.

They have various names among the ancient Writers; after *Pieter de Brueis* <note>Peter of Bruys</note>, they were called *Pedro-Brusianen* <note>Petrobrusians</note>; after *Hendrik de Brueis* <note>Henry of Lausanne, a reformist monk</note>, *Henricianen* <note>Henricians</note>; after *Arnold* <note>Arnold of Brescia</note>, *Arnoldisten* <note>Arnoldists</note>; and because of the purity of their behavior and way of life, they were called *Catharen* <note>Cathars, from the Greek word for "pure"</note>, *Puritains* <note>Puritans</note>, and *Goede Lieden* <note>Good Folk or "Bons Hommes"</note>. They were also sometimes called *Pataryns*, or *Patarinen* <note>Patarines</note>, which according to *Sigonius* <note>Carlo Sigonio (1524–1584), an Italian scholar</note> originated from a small place in the Milanese territory called *Pataro*, where they first revealed themselves. They were also called *Vaudoizen* <note>Waldenses</note>, with whom they formed a community: indeed, one must conclude from both ancient and later Writers that they were one and the same; although perhaps the name *Vaudoizon* was of a more general extent than that of *Albigensen* <note>Albigenses</note>, it is at least certain that they lived in the same places in *Provence* and *Languedoc*, taught the same doctrine, and also had to endure and undergo the same slanders and persecutions: and the learned Jesuit *Gretser* <note>Jacob Gretser (1562–1625)</note> may rightly say that the *Inquisiteurs* <note>Inquisitors</note> often confused the *Albigensen* and *Vaudoizen* with one another, just as *Heer de Maria* <note>Pierre de Marca (1594–1662), a French historian and bishop</note> and others have also done, as can be seen from the aforementioned account. # Alphabetical List of Names: AL

...[origi]nated in the latter part of the 12th century, when *Peter Waldo* <note>Petrus Waldus (c. 1140 – c. 1205), a wealthy merchant from Lyon who gave away his property and began preaching a life of poverty</note> rose up in *Lyon*; but this is not so certain. *Pilichdorf* <note>Peter of Pilichdorf, a 14th-century writer known for his treatises against the Waldensians</note>, a writer of that time, writes that the *Waldensians* are named after a city in *France* called *Walden*, and revealed themselves in the year 1130, and thus long before *Waldo*. It is also very probable that they received their name earlier from *Valdo*, that great friend of *Berengarius* <note>Berengar of Tours (c. 999–1088), a theologian who famously disputed the doctrine of transubstantiation</note>.

In a short time, they filled not only *Provence* and *Languedoc*, but also all the surrounding Provinces, and even penetrated into *Spain*, primarily into *Aragon*. No sooner had they revealed themselves than they were persecuted. The Abbot of *Castres* began the work, but he was halted by the secular authorities. In the 12th century, *Peter of Bruys* <note>Pieter de Brueis, a popular reformer who was eventually lynched by a mob for burning crosses</note> rose up, having previously been a *Roman Priest*, but after a ministry of 20 years, he was burned in the year 1126. The *Albigensians* began to cause the Pope to fear; he sent a Legate <note>a personal representative of the Pope</note> to *France*, and specifically to *Toulouse*, to restrain those heretics, and he also had *Henry of Bruys* <note>Hendrik de Brueis, also known as Henry of Lausanne, a prominent critic of the corruption in the Church</note> secretly burned. But just as it has been in all times, so it was there as well: "the blood of the martyrs was the seed of the Church" <note>This refers to the famous phrase by the early Christian author Tertullian: *Sanguis martyrum semen christianorum*</note>. For through the perseverance of these martyrs, the people began to be moved: and neither the *sermons of St. Bernard* <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), one of the most influential monks and preachers of the Middle Ages</note>, nor his alleged *miracles*—such as using a blessed *Host* <note>the bread or wafer used in the Eucharist</note> to supposedly cure all kinds of diseases—nor all the curses of the Pope and the Councils, nor secret violence, could halt their progress.

->### Alphabetical List of Heretics. 29<-

The cities of *Toulouse*, *Albi*, *Carcassonne*, *Béziers*, *Agde*, *Castres*, *Lavaur*, and all the countryside and cities of *Languedoc* <note>a historical region in southern France where the Albigensian movement was most prominent</note> adopted the teachings of the *Albigensians*, which caused the persecutions to increase. There, use was made of the water ordeal <note>original: *waterproef*; an ancient judicial practice where the accused was thrown into water; it was believed that the pure element of water would reject the guilty, causing them to float</note>; also used to test witches, it was employed there to investigate who were heretics. Those who floated on the water were heretics and had to be put to death, but those who sank were free <note>proving their innocence through the "acceptance" of the water</note>. In the year 1176, the Legate <note>a high-ranking diplomat representing the Pope</note> of the Pope took to the field with a large army. He besieged *Lavaur* and captured it. In this same year, the *Bishops* from around *Toulouse* gathered at *Lombers*, where the *Albigensians* did appear, though they would not recognize that assembly as their judge. Instead, they made the previously noted confession before the people and were condemned. In the following year, the Legate came to *Toulouse*, where he sought and found various heretics whom he excommunicated and drove out of the city.

In the year 1179, Pope *Alexander* <note>Pope Alexander III, who reigned from 1159 to 1181</note>—who had already previously caused the *Albigensians* to be condemned at the Council of *Tours* in France in his presence—convened a Council in the Church of the Lateran in *Rome*. There, he once again condemned them—not because they were *Manichaeans* <note>followers of a dualistic belief system that the Church used as a label for heretics to justify harsher punishments</note>, but as people who made a public confession of their faith and remained in *Albi*—along with the *Patarines* <note>a name given to various groups that opposed the wealth and corruption of the clergy</note>, who are *Waldensians*, and he pronounced a curse upon them. Every morning at the break of day, Mass was celebrated; immediately after, three types of men appeared, well-equipped for the work they were tasked to perform: some to tear down the houses, others to uproot the vineyards and trees, and the third to destroy the sown crops. *Toulouse* could not endure this and therefore fell once again under the *Roman Church*, and *Raymond the Younger*, then Count, fell into the power of the Queen; after which, to do penance, he was forced to wage war against the *Saracens* <note>a medieval term for Muslims, referring here to the Crusades in the Holy Land or Spain</note> for five years.

**ANGELICANS, ANGELICI**, were heretics so named because they worshiped the angels. It seems that this heresy already took its beginning in the time of the *Apostles*; however, it ceased with the *Melchisedecians* <note>A sect that held Melchizedek, the biblical priest-king, to be a divine power greater than Christ</note> around the year 180. *Augustine, Heresy 39* and *Epiphanius, Heresy 6* are of the opinion that they taught that the *World* was made by the *Angels*, or perhaps they were named so because they boasted of leading a life like that of the *Angels*, or because they came from a certain place on the other side of *Mesopotamia* called *Angelina*. However, it seems that there were two kinds of heretics of this name, since the latter ones mentioned by *Epiphanius* only arose in the 3rd century, and thus must be distinguished from the former. *Baronius, year of Christ 360, number 69.*

**ANGELITES**, certain heretics who followed *Sabellius* <note>A 3rd-century priest who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but merely different "modes" or "faces" of one God</note>; they took this name after a place in *Alexandria* called *Agelius* or *Angelius*, where they gathered together. *Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 49.*

# Alphabetical List of Names: AN

**ANTHROPOMORPHITES** <note>literally "those who give human form"</note>, named after one of the leaders of their sect called Audius <note>original Dutch: *Audeus*</note>, also called Audians <note>original Dutch: *Audeanen*</note>, were of the opinion that God had a physical or human form, according to which He had created man. They celebrated Easter in the Jewish manner <note>the practice of celebrating Easter on the 14th of Nisan, the same day as Passover</note>, and fell into the error of the Manichaeans <note>a dualistic religion teaching a struggle between light and darkness</note>, claiming that all things arose from darkness, fire, and water, yet that these things were not created by God. They separated themselves from the other Christian congregations under the pretext that there were many ungodly and impure people among them. The first followers of this Audius were the Egyptian monks. *Epiphanius, Heresies 70. Augustine, Heresies 50.*

**ANTIDICOMARIANITES** <note>literally "opponents of Mary"</note>, was the name given to those heretics <note>literally "spirits of error"</note> who denied the virginity of Mary and claimed that after the birth of the Lord, she bore children with Joseph. This error was introduced by one Helvidius around the end of the 4th century, which is why these heretics are also called Helvidians. *Epiphanius, Heresies 78. Augustine, Heresies 56 & 84. Jerome, Against Helvidius. Baronius, Year of Christ 373.*

**ANTINOMIANS** <note>literally "those against the law"</note>, heretics thus named because they rejected the Law <note>specifically the moral laws of the Old Testament</note>, considering it to be of no use under the Gospel. ### ANTITACTS <note>From the Greek word for "Opponents"</note>, a certain kind of heretics in the 2nd century, sprouted from the *Gnostics*, who believed that *God* had made everything within Himself well and good, but that one of His *creatures* had sown weeds in the world and brought it about that evil appeared. **ANTITRINITARIANS**, a name commonly given to all those who deny the **Holy Trinity**, especially the **Socinians** <note>Followers of the 16th-century Italian theologians Lelio and Fausto Sozzini, who denied the full divinity of Christ</note>, who call themselves **Unitarians**. *Sandius* <note>Christopher Sandius (1644–1680), an Arian historian</note> published a *Library of the Antitrinitarians* <note>original Latin: *Bibliotheca Antitrinitariorum*</note>, containing a list of all the works of the **Unitarians**.

**APELLITES**, certain heretics of the 2nd century and disciples of **Apelles**, who was himself a disciple of **Marcion** <note>A famous early Christian heretic who rejected the Old Testament</note>. He was of the opinion that there were two Gods: one good and one evil, of which the first <note>the evil one, according to his early view</note> had created the **world** and given the **law**; the other was the founder of the **Gospel** and the **Redeemer** of the world. He held this error in common with his master **Marcion**; however, having been expelled from his assembly due to some carnal dealings, he devised another heresy, or rather taught the same from **Philumena**, a possessed girl whom he claimed had an inspiration from the **Holy Spirit**. He then still proposed two Gods, but suggested that the one who was good and the most prominent had also made the evil one. He rejected the **law** and the **Prophets**, and attributed to **Christ** an aerial body <note>meaning a body made of the elements of the air rather than human flesh</note>, of which, when He ascended to Heaven, He had returned to each element its portion. He also denied the bodily resurrection. The Church Fathers strongly refuted these errors. *Epiphanius, Heresies 44. Augustine, chapter 23, On Heresies. Daneau on this passage. Tertullian, On the Prescription of Heretics, chapters 30, 31. Eusebius, book 3, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 13. Baronius, Annals, year 146. Ittig, On the Heresiarchs.* <note>These references cite various early Christian scholars and historians who chronicled and argued against these sects.</note>

# APOLLINARIANS

**APOLLINARIANS** were the name given to the followers of the heretic *Apollinarius*. He was a native of *Laodicea*, a son of *Apollinaris* the Elder, and a student of *Epiphanius* the *Sophist*. He first taught *Logic* <note>original Dutch: *Redeneerkunde*</note>, later became *Rector*, and finally *Bishop of Laodicea*. He flourished around the year 370 and was at first devoted to the orthodox Church, but later fell into certain errors. *George* <note>original: *Georgius*</note>, *Bishop of Laodicea*, is said to have given cause for this; he was an *Arian* <note>A follower of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being and not equal to God the Father</note> who persecuted *Apollinarius* for being a friend of *Athanasius* <note>The Bishop of Alexandria and chief defender of Trinitarian orthodoxy against Arianism</note>.

Because of this, *Apollinarius* was said to have been moved to found his own *Sect*, as he taught that Christ had brought his *human nature* with him from Heaven, and that He had possessed a soul of His own which had been constantly united with His essence; yet, he claimed He no longer possessed it, but the *Godhead* <note>The divine nature of Christ</note> had taken the place of the soul. He taught that Christ was mortal and had suffered according to the *Godhead*; also that the *Godhead* had died and was raised again by the Father. 

When he began to spread this doctrine is uncertain, though it is likely that he was not its first inventor, as some of these doctrines were already rejected at the *Council of Chalcedon* <note>The text cites the year 362; however, the Great Council of Chalcedon occurred in 451. The author likely refers to the Council of Alexandria held in 362, which addressed similar Christological issues</note> in the year 362. *Apollinarius* was also condemned for this, particularly at the *Council of Rome*, which was held in the year 373, or as others would have it, in the year 377 or 378. However, he remained steadfast in his opinion and died under the Emperor *Theodosius*. He was a learned man and wrote extensively, such as

**ARABICS**, or **ARABICI**, Heretics <note>A term used by the author for groups deviating from established church doctrine</note> who arose in the 3rd century. <header>History of the Heretics. 47</header>

The beginning of **Arianism** was brought about by certain differences that *Alexander*, Bishop of Alexandria, had with *Arius*, one of his Priests, regarding the Divinity of *Jesus Christ*. To properly understand what these differences consisted of, one must necessarily examine the matter from a higher perspective and investigate the foundation of the *philosophy* used among Christians at that time, and how it had been introduced. This is a necessary digression, as will become apparent in what follows.

There has been no philosophy that has made itself so famous as that of *Plato*, and there have been no books read with as much pleasure as his, whether due to the *subjects* and the elevated thoughts found within them, or due to the purity and sublimity of their style. He was born under the reign of *Artaxerxes*, nicknamed *Longhand* <note>Artaxerxes I, often called *Longimanus* in Latin texts</note>, 426 years before Christ, and died at 80 years old. This was during the time when *Philip of Macedon*, who made all of Greece fear him, had a son named *Alexander* <note>Alexander the Great</note> who made himself master of *Asia*. Because his successors divided that realm among themselves, one can easily believe that the Greek sciences established themselves there along with their government and customs. *Ptolemy*, the son of *Lagus* <note>Ptolemy I Soter, founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt</note>, one of the successors of *Alexander*, collected as many books as possible in his Library in *Alexandria*, and he lured several scholars from Greece to that place.

<summary>This page explains that understanding the Arian controversy requires looking at the influence of Platonic philosophy in Alexandria, tracing the spread of Greek thought from the conquests of Alexander the Great to the establishment of the Great Library by Ptolemy.</summary>

His Son *Philadelphus* <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus</note> followed here in his Father's footsteps. One may also believe that *Asia*, which was then filled with Greek Philosophers, had no lack of *Platonists*.

Among the views of *Plato*, none are more noteworthy than those he held regarding *Divinity*, *Pre-existence*, and the *Immortality of the Soul*. He believed that there was but one *supreme, spiritual, and invisible God*, whom he calls *the Being*, or *Being itself*, *the Good itself*, the *Father* and the *Origin* of all *Beings*, etc. Beneath this supreme God, he placed a lesser *Being*, which he calls *the Word* <note>original: Λόγος (*Logos*)</note>, the *Governor* of present and future affairs, the *Creator* of the universe, etc. Finally, he recognized a third *Being*, which he calls *the Spirit*, or the *Soul of the World*. He added further that the first was the *Father* of the second, and that the second had brought forth the third. One may consult his *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato's most influential dialogues, dealing with the nature of the physical world and the creator</note> regarding this, to which one must add his second and sixth Letter. See here what his doctrine amounts to. 1. There are three causes: *The Being* <note>Refers to "The One," the supreme, transcendent source in Neoplatonism</note>, *the Mind* <note>original: *de Geeſt*; representing the *Nous* or Divine Intellect</note>, or *the word of the Being*, and *the World Soul*, which is the *Word* of the *Mind*. The second matter to which one must pay attention is that, in such a difficult subject, one must be satisfied with what they positively state, without attempting to draw far-fetched consequences from their principles, which can only be half-understood. Otherwise, one would run the risk of attributing thoughts to them which they never held.

One should not even attempt to reconcile the contradictions in such an abstract Subject that might seem to be found in their teachings, nor conclude that they could not have understood matters in any certain way because, if that were the case, they would have contradicted themselves. It was the custom of these *Philosophers* <note>Dutch: *Philosophen*</note> that they seemed to contradict themselves in a certain way by using the same expressions in different senses. Moreover, it is easy to understand that they might sometimes have been able to contradict themselves in a matter of which they had no distinct idea <note>Dutch: *onderſcheiden denkbeeld*—a clear and discrete concept</note>.

A second *Dogma of the Platonists*, which has caused much stir, is that of the *pre-existence of souls in the sublunar places* <note>In ancient cosmology, the "sublunar" realm was the region of the cosmos below the moon, subject to change and decay, as opposed to the eternal celestial spheres.</note> (see the *Timaeus of Plato*), of the misdeeds they might have committed there, of their banishment from this happy residence to come dwell in bodies that are arranged in a different manner according to the various merits of these Souls; and finally of the *return to the places* from where they took their *origin*.

The Kings of *Egypt* and *Syria*, having brought the sciences of the Greeks into *Asia*, the *Jews*, who were numerous in these two Kingdoms and were obliged to interact with them, learned their views from them, and made no difficulty in embracing those which did not seem to conflict with their Religion. One should not wonder at this diversity <note>Referring to the conflicting reports from different historians regarding the Council’s proceedings.</note>, as there are few places in *Church History* where one can observe more confusion and negligence than in the history of this famous *Council*. One has also been obliged to draw what will be said about it from various historical writers, because none of the ancients gave a complete account of it. With respect to the diversity noted among historians regarding the same matter, the oldest sources have been followed here, or those with the greatest probability. *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), often called the "Father of Church History."</note>, who was present at this *Council*, only touched upon the circumstances of this history in passing, possibly out of fear of offending the *Arians* or the *Orthodox*. Since then, this matter has never been spoken of with complete neutrality, and rumors have often been recounted as truth.

[The council] had to condemn the notion that the *Son* was brought forth out of nothing, that he was a creature, that there had been a time when he did not exist, etc., and instead make use of the idioms of Scripture, such as these: that the *Son is unique by his nature*, that he is the *Word*, the *Power*, and the *Wisdom* of his *Father*, the *reflection of his glory*, and the *exact image of his substance* <note>original: "zelfstandigheid"; a translation of the Greek *hypostasis* or Latin *substantia*, referring to the fundamental nature of God.</note>. Therefore, they wanted to add that the *Son is of the substance of the Father*, because this is what distinguishes the *Son* from the creatures.

Regarding this, the *Arians* were asked whether they did not agree that the *Son* is no creature, but the *Power*, the *only Wisdom*, and the *Image of the Father*; that he is *eternal*, and in *all things equal* to the *Father*, and finally *truly God*. The unorthodox, having spoken with one another, thought that these expressions could very well correspond with the idea they had of the divinity of the Son, and indicated that they were ready to accept them. 

Finally, since it had been noted that *Eusebius of Nicomedia* <note>Eusebius of Nicomedia was the primary political supporter of Arius and a key figure in the early Arian controversy.</note> in the letter that had been read rejected the expression *consubstantial* <note>original: "medezelfstandig"; this is the Dutch translation for the Greek term *homoousios*, meaning "of the same substance." <meta>This page continues the analysis of the Council of Nicaea (325 AD) and the specific language used in the Nicene Creed to oppose Arianism. It follows the previous discussion of Eusebius of Caesarea's initial hesitation to accept the term "Consubstantial."</meta>

# ...of the Heretics.

...had been begotten; *Eusebius* and others asserted that the expressions of the *Creed* <note>original: "Symbolum"; the formal statement of Christian belief</note> and of the *Anathemas* <note>original: "Anathemaas"; formal curses or excommunications against heretical views</note> should be explained. 

1. It is said that the word *Begotten* <note>original: "Gegenereert"</note> was used, and not that of *Made*, because this latter word signifies the production of creatures, to which the *Son* has no likeness, being of a much more glorious *Substance* <note>original: "Zelfstandigheid"; in this context, it refers to the Greek "ousia" or the essential nature of God</note> than they, begotten by the *Father* in an incomprehensible manner. 

2. The word *Consubstantial* <note>original: "Medezelfstandig"; the Dutch equivalent of the Greek "homoousios"</note> is proper to the *Son*; not in the sense in which it is used when one speaks of bodies, or of mortal animals; the *Son* not being *consubstantial* with the *Father* through a division of the *Divine Substance*, of which he would possess a part, nor through a change of that same *Substance*. By this, one means nothing else than that the *Son* has no similarity to the creatures he brought forth, but that he is equal in all things to his *Father*, by whom he was begotten, or that he is of no other existence or substance, but of that of his *Father*.

3. They condemned those who said that the *Son* did not exist before he was born, since he existed before his physical birth, and even before his *Divine* generation, according to the reasoning of *Eusebius*. This will perhaps seem like pure *Arianism* <note>original: "Arianerey"; the belief that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father</note>, and a denial of the eternity of the **Son**; but one must note that, in the style of that time, to exist before the world and to be eternal are the same thing; because to prove his eternity one brings up this passage, *In the beginning was the Word*, and one is satisfied to show that he was begotten <note>original: "gegenereert"</note> before there was any time. Thus one must not reject these words as fabricated solely for this reason; and it is so common to find harsh expressions among those who have tried in some way to express this incomprehensible mystery, that if one were to judge them by that, one would have to declare them all *Heretics*, that is to say, pronounce the *Anathema* <note>original: "Anathema"; a formal curse or decree of excommunication used by the Church</note> over the greater part of the ancients. Besides this, **St. Athanasius**, who openly considers **Eusebius** an *Arian* (*On the Decrees of Nicaea <note>original: "De decret. Niceen."</note>, Vol. 1, page 251*), alludes to a part of this passage and draws a conclusion from it that **Eusebius** would undoubtedly never have acknowledged: that the *Arians* believed the Divinity of **Jesus Christ** did not exist before his bodily birth.

After these explanations, **Eusebius** signed—as he himself testifies in the letter that has been produced—although he had refused to do so the previous day. ***Constantia***, sister of ***Constantine*** and widow of ***Licinius***, had among her household a Priest who was a friend of ***Arius*** and shared his views. They added that they had only refused to condemn *Arius* because they knew that he was not as he was described; and that, since this had been recognized by recalling him from exile, it would not be fair that they, who suffered for his sake, remained banished after his recall."

This letter was addressed to the principal bishops, whom they begged to speak for them to the Emperor. Speaking of the recall of *Arius*, they attributed it to these bishops: *Your compassion*, they said, *has seen fit to treat him gently and to recall him.* A learned man (*Valesius* <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century French scholar and editor of ancient church histories</note> *in his commentary on this passage*) remarks on this place that *Eusebius* and *Theognis* attribute to the bishops that which the Emperor had done, since it was he who had recalled *Arius*; and that ecclesiastical historians also sometimes attribute to the Emperor the actions of the bishops. For example, when *Socrates* <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian</note> says that the *Council of Nicaea* forbade *Arius* from entering *Alexandria* again, whereas it was actually the Emperor who did so. But the truth is that the Emperor at that time little <note>The sentence continues on the next page: "...did little [without the advice of the bishops]."</note>

In the year 359, a *Council* was assembled at *Seleucia*, and at the same time another at *Rimini*. The leaders of the *Arians*, judging that they would better achieve their goal if the *Easterners* were separated from the *Westerners*; obtained from the Emperor *Constantius*, who was then at *Sirmium*, that the *Bishops* be divided into two *Councils*, and that those of the *East* should gather at *Seleucia*, while those of the *West* held their *Council* at *Rimini*, a city in *Italy*. But the Emperor commanded them at the same time to jointly draft a *Confession of Faith*, in order to present it to both the *Councils*. They created one, which entailed that when speaking of God and of his *Son*, they would abolish the expression of *substance* <note>original: "zelffstandigheid"</note>, and that it was true that the *Son* is like his *Father*, in all things.

ATHEISTS are those who do not posit a God, or at least have no Religion. *Atheists* are also those called who *lead a Godless life*, and do not concern themselves with Piety or honesty.

BAANITES were Heretics who had their origin from a certain *Baanes*, who presented himself as a *Disciple* of *Epaphroditus*, and spread the errors of the *Manichaeans* <note>The Manichaeans followed a dualistic religion teaching a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note> in the 9th century. <note>original Latin: *Petr. **BASILIDIANS**, named as such after the Heretic *Basilides*, who was a Disciple of *Simon the Sorcerer* <note>Also known as Simon Magus, a figure from the New Testament often cited by early church writers as the first heretic and the father of Gnosticism.</note>; he lived in the second century and expanded his teachings in *Egypt*. He denied the *Trinity*, and taught much concerning the various origins of the *Angels*, by whom a total of 365 *Heavens* were created, which he encompassed under the name of *Abraxas* <note>A mystical word found in Gnostic texts; in Greek gematria, the letters of Abraxas add up to 365, representing the days of the year or the levels of heaven.</note>, understanding thereby the eternal God. To the lowest sort of his *Angels* he attributed the creation of the earth and of mankind. Among these, he called the most prominent one the *God of the Jews*. He said that God had sent *Christ*, as his only-begotten Son, into the world to deliver mankind from the *Dominion of the Angels*, but this *Christ* had not suffered; rather, it was *Simon of Cyrene* <note>The man who helped carry the cross of Jesus; Basilides claimed Simon was transformed to look like Jesus and died in his place.</note>. Because of this, *Basilides* disparaged the death of the *Martyrs*, saying that in times of persecution one might freely renounce the faith. He maintained that *Souls* had sinned in another life and were punished for it in this one, because God forgave no sins except those committed through *ignorance*. Furthermore, he denied the *resurrection of the flesh*, and for that reason permitted his Followers all fleshly desires. He and his disciples used all manner of strange words, figures, and *Characters* <note>Mystical symbols or sigils used in ritual magic.</note>, with which they practiced their *Sorcery*. **BEGHARDS**, and **BEGUINES**, were Heretics who took their origin in the *Netherlands* at the end of the 13th century. They lived unmarried, and taught that man can reach ultimate perfection without sinning in this life; that one then had no need to fast or pray; and because the outward feeling was entirely subject to the Spirit, one could allow the body whatever one wanted, without such a person needing to be subject to any human Ordinances. They had a large following in *Germany*, but were first condemned in the year 1166 at the *Council in Vienna* <note>The date 1166 in the source appears to be an error, as it precedes the 13th-century origin mentioned; this may refer to a local synod or a misprint for a later council.</note>, afterwards in the year 1260 in *Cologne*, and finally at the general Council of *Vienne*, in *France* in the year 1311.

The **BEGUINES** consisted of *Women*, and were divided into two kinds. The first took no monastic vows, following the errors of the Beghards, and of *Margaret Porete* <note>A French mystic and author of "The Mirror of Simple Souls," executed for heresy in 1310.</note>. The others were not condemned, living according to the institutions prescribed for them by *St. Begga*, Sister of *St. Gertrude*, or as others maintain, by a certain Priest *Lambert le Bègue* <note>The nickname "le Bègue" means "the Stammerer."</note>. Pope *John* XXII made a distinction between these two kinds; thus today the remains of the

### **BOGOMILS**,
so certain heretics were named in the 12th century, who are said to have denied the **Holy Trinity** and attributed a *human* nature to God. They taught that the **World** was created by the evil angels; they also boasted of having the *Baptism* of Christ, while the rest of Christendom only had the Baptism of *John*. The *Lord's Prayer* they called the *Holy Supper*; they also believed in no other Resurrection than that which occurred through repentance and a Christian life, etc. They also rejected the *veneration* of the Saints and the sacrifice of the *Mass*. However, writers do not agree with one another regarding these Bogomils. It is also held that *Bogomili* in the Slavonic language <note>Specifically Old Church Slavonic; "Bogu milui" roughly translates to "God have mercy."</note> means someone who calls upon the mercy of God; for they were considered very holy people. *Johann Christoph Wolf* published the *History of these Bogomils in Quarto* in the year 1712. *Zygabenus, <note>original: "Zygabenus in dogmat. Panoplia"</note> in the Full Armor of Doctrine, part 2, title 23; Anna Comnena, <note>original: "Anna Comnena de gestis Alexii Commeni"</note> On the Deeds of Alexios Komnenos, book 15; Baronius for the year of Christ 1118; Prateolus; Sanderus; Kortholt, *Ecclesiastical History, 12th Century, Chapter 2.*

mixed with Adamites and *Waldensians*. They were actually *Hussites*, refusing to accept the decrees of the *Council of Basel* <note>A 15th-century church council that attempted to address the Hussite wars and ecclesiastical reforms.</note>. After they lost the battle against the *Bohemian Nobility* in the year 1434, and their General *Procopius* <note>Prokop the Great, a prominent Hussite leader who died at the Battle of Lipany.</note> was killed, they held their meetings either in the wilderness, or in *caves*, or in *private houses*, and were therefore called *Speluncales* <note>Latin: "cave dwellers"</note> and *Jamnici* <note>from the Slavic "jamníci," meaning "pit-dwellers"</note>. Finally, King *George Podiebrad* <note>George of Poděbrady, the first non-Catholic king of Bohemia.</note> gave them the Land of *Lititz*, located on the borders of *Silesia* and *Moravia*, where they performed their worship primarily in the village of *Kunwald*, calling themselves *Brothers* and *Sisters* among one another. Later, many prominent families from *Bohemia* and *Moravia* joined them, at which time, under King *Vladislaus* the fourth, they again received various *Churches* and expanded into the neighboring lands.

When *Luther* arose, they sent two *Emissaries* to him, testifying that they were at one with him regarding the matter of doctrine, and had some of his writings translated into the *Bohemian language*. In the year 1535, they submitted their *Confessions of Faith* to the Emperor, which came to light in the year 1538 with a preface by *Luther*. Because they refused to send aid to King *Ferdinand* for the *Schmalkaldic War* <note>A 16th-century war between the Holy Roman Empire and a league of Lutheran princes.</note> after this, their churches were closed in the year 1547 and their *Preachers* were driven out. Thus, many of these Brothers departed for *Poland*, *Prussia*, *Transylvania* <note>original: "Zevenbergen"</note>, and *Switzerland*, partially embracing the views of the *Lutherans* and partially those of the *Reformed*. ### BORELISTS

, a certain type of Christians in Holland, so named after *Adam Boreel*, a Zeelander <note>A native of the Dutch province of Zeeland.</note> by birth, and infected with Socinianism <note>Socinianism was a rationalist Christian movement that denied the Trinity and the divinity of Christ.</note>, but otherwise a learned man, and very experienced in the Hebrew language. He wrote a work under the title of *To the Law and the Testimony* <note>original: "ad legem & testimonium"</note>, against which *Hoornbeek*, *Maresius*, and others have written. Furthermore, there is from him in the Dutch language, *Golden Christian Concatenation* <note>original: "Concatenatio aurea Christiana"</note>, and *Treatise on the Fraternal Religion* <note>original: "Tractatus de fraterna Religione"</note>. He died in the year 1666; his followers were called Borelists in Holland, of whom Mr. *Stoup* gives an account in his treatise on the *Religion of the Dutch*. Their way of life is very strict, and they spend most of their goods on alms; they care neither for sacraments, public prayers, nor any other public worship. When reading the *Holy Scripture*, they also will not tolerate any human interpretations. *Sandius* in *Library of the Anti-Trinitarians* <note>original: "Bibl. ## BROWNISTS

This is the name given to a certain religious group that emerged in England during the 16th century, and who are also counted among the Independents. They are said to have their origin with *Robert Bolton*, who was the very first in England to separate himself over the matter of Church governance. After him, *Robert Brown* joined them; he was first a preacher in *London*, and it is from him that they received their name. He traveled from *England* to *Middelburg* in *Zeeland*, but later returned and recanted his opinions, being received back into the *English Church* <note>The Church of England or Anglican Church.</note>. Following this, *Henry Barrow* joined the group, though he, along with his associate *Greenwood*, was put to death in the year 1593 by order of Queen *Elizabeth*. The *Brownists* called them *Martyrs*, and relocated from *England* to *Amsterdam*, where they had two leaders, *Francis Johnson* and *Henry Ainsworth*, who published their confession of faith in the year 1602. After these events, some stayed in *Emden*, *Leiden*, and elsewhere, while some remained in *England*. *John Robinson* was held in high esteem among them, writing an *Apology* <note>original: "Apologie"; a formal written defense of one's religious position.</note> for himself and his followers. Regarding their way of life, they themselves confess that they agree with the *Reformed Church* on the primary *Articles of Faith*, but they reject the *English Church governance*, the *heathen names* <note>The Brownists objected to using names for days of the week (like Thursday/Thor or Friday/Frigg) that were derived from pagan gods.</note> of the days, and the reading of *heathen books* <note>This refers to the use of classical Greek and Roman literature in education, which some radical reformers viewed as worldly or corrupting.</note>. Others attribute further errors to them, namely, that they reject both *Episcopal* <note>Governance by bishops.</note> and *Presbyterian* <note>Governance by elders or presbyters.</note> church government, at least in the latter

### C.

**CAINITES**, **CAINIANS**, were certain Heretics, a type of *Gnostics*, in the 2nd century after the birth of Christ. They derived their name from *Cain*, whom they claimed was formed by a *heavenly* and *Almighty power*, whereas *Abel*, on the contrary, was said to have been made by a much weaker power. They believed that the way to salvation consisted in seeking to experience all kinds of things and seeking to follow one’s desires in all manner of wicked undertakings. They held various ridiculous opinions regarding a great number of Angels, to whom they gave *Barbarian Names* <note>This refers to non-Greek, often Hebrew-sounding magical names used in Gnostic rituals</note>, and to each of whom they attributed a specific sin. Thus, if they were caught in a bad deed, they pleaded for help from that Angel who, in their opinion, was set over it. They forged a godless book under the title of the *Ascension of St. Paul*, which they presented as the secret words that the Apostle had heard during his ecstasy <note>Referring to the biblical account of Paul being "caught up to the third heaven"</note>. They also showed a singular respect for *Cain*, *Korah* <note>original: "Coran"</note>, *Dathan*, *Abiram* <note>Biblical figures who famously rebelled against the authority of Moses</note>, the *Sodomites*, and especially for *Judas*, because his betrayal had caused the death of Christ: They also made use of a certain *Gospel* bearing the name of this false Apostle. *Tertullian, On the Prescription of Heretics* <note>original Latin: "de præsc."</note> *chapters 33, 47, etc. Jerome* <note>original Latin: "Hironym."</note> *book 1, chapter 34. Epiphanius, Against Heresies* <note>original Latin: "hæreſ."</note> *38. Augustine, chapter 18, On Heresies* <note>original Latin: "de her."</note>. *Baronius, Year of Christ 145* <note>original Latin: "a. C. 145"</note>.

**CALIXTINES**, this was the name given in the 17th century to the **Helmstedt** theologians and others who sided with **Calixtus** <note>Georg Calixtus (1586–1656), a German Lutheran theologian who sought to find common ground between Lutherans, Catholics, and Calvinists.</note> and his followers on certain *Theological Points of Dispute* against the **Wittenbergers**. In several points, they conceded more to the **Roman Catholics** than the latter did, for which reason they were also accused by the *Wittenbergers* of **Syncretism** <note>The attempt to reconcile or combine different, even contradictory, religious beliefs into a single system.</note>.

**CAMERONIANS**, a sect of **Presbyterians** in **Scotland**, so named after **Archibald Cameron** <note>Though the author writes Archibald, this refers to the movement associated with Richard Cameron (1648–1680), a militant leader of the Scottish Covenanters.</note>, a field preacher and the first to separate himself from the communion of other *Presbyterians* regarding ministers whose views did not match his own. These others had accepted the **liberty of conscience** granted by **Charles II**, which he <note>Cameron</note> argued gave ground to the right of **Royal Supremacy** <note>original Dutch: "Opperhoofdigheid"; the doctrine that the King is the supreme head of the Church.</note> which this Prince claimed to have over the Church. They, on the contrary, maintained that they had done nothing but use the **Liberty** granted to them to practice the **Duties** of a **Minister**, which had been unjustly hindered. The dispute grew with much vehemence on both sides; however, other *Presbyterians* were of the opinion that this should be left to rest until the disagreement could be decided by a general **Assembly**.

### CATAPHRYGES
This was the name given to the **Montanists**, or followers of **Montanus**, in the second century, because the heresy of **Montanus** first revealed itself in **Phrygia**. <note>The Montanists were an early Christian movement that emphasized new prophetic revelations and strict moral discipline. Phrygia is a region in ancient Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note> *Epiphanius, Heresy 48. Augustine, Heresy 26. Baronius, Year of Christ 163.*

### CATHARI
This was the name given to some among the **Novatians**, who boasted that they were purer than others. <note>The name "Cathari" is derived from the Greek *katharos*, meaning "pure." The Novatians were a rigorist group who refused to readmit Christians who had renounced their faith under Roman persecution.</note> **Augustine** testifies that they forbade second marriages, further asserting with **Novatus** <note>Also known as Novatian (c. 200–258), a Roman priest and antipope who founded the Novatianist sect.</note> that those who had once renounced the faith after Baptism were beyond repentance. In later times, the **Albigensians**, **Waldensians**, **Arnoldists**, and others were also called **Cathari** <note>Referring to the medieval "Cathar" movement in Europe.</note> in order to make them loathsome; and some believe that the word heretic [Dutch: *Ketter*], like the High German **Katzer** <note>Modern German: *Ketzer*.</note>, has its origin in **Cathari**, or perhaps from **Gazari**. <note>The term "Gazari" likely refers to the Khazars or other Balkan groups who were often conflated with heretical sects by medieval authorities.</note> *Eusebius, Book 9, Chapter 35. Socrates, Book 6, Chapter 20. Augustine, On Heresies, Chapter 38. & Danaeus on this passage. Baronius, Year of Christ 254. Raynaldus, Spondanus, Arnold’s History of Heretics.*

### CHILIASTS

## COLARBASUS

A certain *Heretic*, living in the second century, who is said to have been a *Disciple of Marcus*, who in turn was a *Disciple of Valentinus*. <note>Valentinus (c. 100–160 AD) was the most influential Gnostic teacher, whose complex systems of "Aeons" and divine emanations were later expanded upon by followers like Marcus and Colarbasus.</note> His propositions for the most part correspond with those of *Valentinus*. He was a lover of *Astronomy* <note>Here referring to astrology, as the distinction was blurred in the ancient world.</note>, teaching that the life and procreation of humans depended on the *Planets*. Furthermore, he sought great mysteries in numbers and letters. <note>This refers to Gnostic gematria, where the numerical values of letters were thought to reveal hidden divine truths.</note> *Irenaeus, Book 1, Chapter 8. Epiphanius, Heresy 31. Author of the appendix to Tertullian, On Prescription, Chapter 30. Augustine, On Heresies, Chapter 15. Daneau on this place. Damascene, On Heresies, Chapter 35. This occurred under the reign of the Emperor *Constans*, who died in the year 350; and it seems that matters remained in this state until *Julian* <note>Known as Julian the Apostate, he reversed many of his predecessors' Christian policies, often to stir up internal conflict among Christian factions.</note> became Emperor. At their request, he ordered that they should be restored and that the churches which had been taken from them should be returned to them. Whereupon, it is said, they reclaimed their churches with great turbulence and committed many acts of violence. However, it happened that they fell into disagreement among themselves, and various factions arose among them, condemning one another in private Church Councils and persecuting each other vehemently. 

Just as they weakened themselves through these divisions, the Orthodox <note>original: "Regtzinnigen"; referring to the state-sanctioned Catholic Church that followed the Nicene Creed.</note> did not fail to refute them through learned writings, among which *Optatus of Milevis* and *Augustine* <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers, spent much of his career writing against the Donatists.</note> were the most prominent. Discussions and meetings were also held with them to convince them orally; added to this were several Church Councils in which they were condemned, as well as some strict laws from the Emperors *Valentinian*, *Gratian*, *Honorius*, and *Theodosius the Younger*, etc. Yet they were not rooted out by these measures, as Pope *Gregory the Great* still complained as late as the sixth century that they had grown significantly through the negligence of the clergy. But after the *Donatists* had dominated *Africa*, the Orthodox were destroyed at the same time as the *Donatists*. <note>This likely refers to the eventual collapse of Christian North Africa following the Vandal and later Islamic conquests, which rendered the internal theological disputes moot.</note>

# PROPONENTS OF THE MILLENNIAL KINGDOM

**PROPONENTS OF THE MILLENNIAL KINGDOM** <note>Historically known as Millennialists or Chiliasts, from the Greek word *chilioi*, meaning thousand</note>, is a certain persuasion whose followers imagine that the blessed, after the general Last Judgment <note>While most Millennialist theories place the thousand-year reign before the final judgment, the author here describes a specific interpretation where it follows the judgment</note>, will remain on the earth for *a thousand years*, where they will enjoy all pleasures and delights of both the body and the spirit. *Papias*, who lived in the second century and was a disciple of *St. John the Evangelist* and Bishop of *Hierapolis*, is considered the founder of this sect. The esteem in which he was held misled several Church Fathers—such as *Irenaeus*, *Justin Martyr*, and *Tertullian*—to adhere to this view, which they firmly established based on a certain passage of Scripture from the *Revelation* of *John*, Chapter 22 <note>Though the text cites Chapter 22, the "millennial kingdom" is most famously described in Revelation Chapter 20</note>, where a *millennial kingdom* is mentioned. Since then, *Nepos*, a Bishop in *Egypt*, maintained this persuasion in the third century with such persistence and eloquence that *Dionysius of Alexandria*, who otherwise held this prelate in great affection, found himself obliged to speak against and refute this doctrine; and *Coracion*, one of the foremost proponents of this view, having been convinced [of his error], abandoned it, being followed in this by nearly all the others. Pope *Damasus* later condemned this doctrine in a *Synod* <note>A formal council of church leaders</note> held at Rome against the *Apollinarists* <note>Followers of Apollinaris of Laodicea, who was accused of teaching a physical or "Jewish" interpretation of the Millennium</note>. *Epiphanius, On Heresies, 77* <note>original: "hær. 77."</note>; *Sanderus, On Heresies, 51* <note>original: "hær. 51."</note>; *Philastrius*; *Baronius, Year of Christ 264, nos. 1, 2* <note>original: "a. C. 264. n. 1. 2."</note>; and *Eusebius, Book 7, chapter 9* <note>original: "Euſeb. lib. 7. c. 9."</note>.

DULCINIANS, thus named after a certain *Dulcinus* <note>Fra Dolcino (c. 1250–1307) was a radical preacher in Italy who led the Apostolic Brethren</note>, who was the leader of this sect in the 14th century. # Alphabetical List of Names
## EB

in *Hebrew* <note>The Hebrew word is *ebyonim* (אביונים)</note> means as much as *poor*, by which name especially those *Jews* who turned to *Christianity* and were converted were called, both because most of them were deprived of *temporal goods* <note>Meaning earthly wealth or possessions</note>, and because they held the poor and *despised Jesus* for the *Messiah*. It is well known that *Irenæus* <note>Irenaeus of Lyons (2nd century AD), an early church father known for his writings against heresy</note> and others before *Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403), who wrote the *Panarion*, a detailed catalog of heresies</note> certainly mention the *Ebionites* but not a leader named *Ebion*, and that the testimony of *Epiphanius* in this matter carries little weight with many. But since *Irenæus* nevertheless places the *Ebionites* among those *heretics* who bear the name of their first leader, one must conclude from this that they were also named after *Ebion*; and although the first *Christians* were mockingly called *Ebionites*, or *poor wretches*, by the *Jews*, as *Origen* <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253), an influential early Christian scholar and theologian</note> notes, it does not follow from this that there were no specific heretics of that name. When *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), the first major historian of the Christian Church</note> also says that the *Ebionites* were named thus because they had truly *poor and wretched views* of *Christ*, he is indeed referring to the meaning of this name, yet he by no means denies that they had their first origin from *Ebion*. Regarding the *Doctrine of the Ebionites*, they are accused of casting doubt on the *Divinity* of *Christ* and siding with the *Jews* in many matters, for which reason they also maintained the necessity of *Circumcision* and the observance of the ancient Laws; all of which sprouted from the fact that they believed *Christ* had come into the world only for the sake of the *Jews*. ELCESAITES, or ELCESEITES, otherwise also called SAMPSEITES, were certain heretics <term>Ketters: individuals holding beliefs at odds with established church doctrine</term> who appeared at the beginning of the second century, having their origin from one *Elcesai*, a *Jew*, who is called *Elxai* and *Elci* by some, and who joined the *Ebionites* <note>A group of early Jewish Christians who insisted on the followance of Jewish Law</note> around the year 114, introducing new doctrines into that sect. *The Elcesaites distinguished, like the Ebionites, the ceremonies of the Law of Moses, as well as circumcision and the Sabbath, but rejected sacrifices. ->**AND of Heretics.**<-

The **Enthusiasts**, the **Quakers**, or the **Tremblers** <note>original: "Bevers," from the Dutch word *beven* (to tremble), a literal translation of the name "Quaker"</note>, says **Mr. Stouppe** <note>likely Jean-Baptiste Stouppe, a 17th-century author who wrote about the various religions in the Netherlands</note>, who believe they are affected by a **Divine infusion**, claim that the **Holy Scripture** must be interpreted through the **Illumination** of this **Divine inspiration**, without which the Bible is nothing more than a dead writing, and that it is not the true, only, and perfect word of God. They maintain that their **Spirit** is much more truly that word, to which one must listen and follow—that **Spirit** which man has within himself and which serves as his Teacher, to point out to him everything that he must believe. They sit still in their **Meetings** for a long time, without speaking and without moving. One hears only a few sighs, until someone among them, feeling the **instigations** and the **movement** of the **Spirit**, stands up and speaks those things which the **Spirit** commands him to say. Even the **Women** feel the movements of the **Spirit**, which causes them, as well as the **Men**, to speak in their **Meetings**.

In their dealings they frequently speak of their **Ecstasies** and **Revelations**. **Caspar Schwenkfeld**, a Nobleman from **Silesia**, was one of the first leaders of these **Fanatics** <term>Geestdryvers: literally "spirit-drivers," a term used historically for "enthusiasts" who claimed direct divine inspiration, often used disparagingly by their critics</term> in the year 1527. He had, by outward appearance, a great piety, and those of his following regarded him as a second Enoch. *Theodoret, Church History.* <note>original: "Theodoretus Histor. Ecclesiast."</note>

### EUDOXIANS were Heretics and followers of *Eudoxius*, an *Arian* <term>Arianism: a belief that Jesus Christ was not co-eternal with God the Father but was a created being</term>, who lived in the fourth century and was a son of *Caesarius* the *Martyr*, born in *Arabissus*, a city in *Lesser Armenia*. First he was Bishop at *Germanicia*; thereafter in the year 356 at *Antioch*, which dignity was stripped from him at the *Council* of *Seleucia*. He favored the *Arians*, as well as—having read the letters of *Asterius*—the *Semi-Arians*, wherefore, having become Bishop of *Constantinople* in the year 360, he made Emperor *Valens*, whom he baptized, swear with a solemn oath that he would expel the orthodox. He passed away in the year 370, having sat upon the See <note>original: "Stoel," literally "chair," referring to the episcopal throne</note> in *Constantinople* for nineteen years according to *Socrates*, but as *Sozomen* says, no more than eleven or twelve years. He taught that the Son was distinct from the Father in His will, and was made out of nothing. *Socrates, Baronius, etc.*

### EUPSYCHIANS
Certain heretics, thus named after *Eupsychius*, who was a *Eunomian* and lived in the fourth century. He left the followers of *Eunomius* due to a dispute regarding the knowledge of *Jesus Christ*. *Sozomen, Book 7, Chapter 17*. *Prateolus*, etc.

### EUSTATHIANS

These were Heretics, named after *Eustathius* <note>likely Eustathius of Sebaste, a bishop in Armenia known for his extreme asceticism</note>, who lived in the 4th century. He was a *Monk*, and so foolishly enamored with his *Profession* <note>the monastic life</note> that he condemned all other states of *Civil Life* and excluded all those who were married from salvation. Under the pretext of leading a more perfect and rigorous life, he taught many wicked errors and established practices that conflicted with the Laws of the Church. The *Bishops* gathered at *Gangra* <note>the Synod of Gangra, held in modern-day Turkey to address these specific radical teachings</note> around the year 370, condemned his errors, such as:

1. *Concerning the condemnation of Marriage, and the separation of Wives from their Husbands.*
2. *Concerning the abandonment of the public Assemblies of the Church, in order to hold private ones instead.*

They imagine that the fair sex will easily allow themselves to be ensnared, and that their inclination for the external practices of religion—and those of nature, which manages to maintain a wonderful harmony with the other—will provide them the means to make the *women* lean toward whatever is desired of them.

## GEORGIANS 
, a type of Christians in the Eastern Church, located between the Caspian Sea and the *Pontus Euxinus* <note>The ancient Greek name for the Black Sea.</note>, who accepted the Christian Faith in the fourth century. According to the writings of *P. Avitabilis* <note>Pietro Avitabile (1595–1650), a missionary who wrote extensively about the religious practices of the Caucasus region.</note>, most Georgians believe that the Unbelievers are judged separately, and that they will not appear at the General Judgment. They work on even the most solemn feast days, including Christmas. During baptism, the Priest delivers a discourse over the child in the water, and thus it is baptized by the Father or a Relative, rather than by the Priest. They also re-baptize those who change their faith if they have previously fallen away. They never perform a baptism without the presence of the Priest, even in cases of greatest necessity, though some of their Teachers believe that the baptism which the Mother received can suffice for the child.

Meanwhile, the historian *Fleury* <note>Claude Fleury (1640–1723) was a highly influential French Roman Catholic priest and ecclesiastical historian.</note> says:

> a movement of *piety* has arisen in *Italy*, the likes of which had never been seen before. This movement had its beginning in *Perugia* <note>original: "Perouse"</note>, moved from there to *Rome*, and further through the entire country. The Noblemen and the common people, the old and the young, even down to children five years of age, struck by the fear of God because of the sins that flooded all of *Italy*, walked through the streets of every city entirely naked, except for those parts that must necessarily be covered for the sake of decency; they walked *in the manner of a procession* two by two, each holding a leather scourge in their hand, and, while *uttering manifold sighs* and *shedding tears*, they struck their shoulders so violently that they became entirely bloody.

Then he adds how they also continued their journey by night with burning *wax candles* in their hands, even in the harshest part of the *winter*. They were seen in groups of hundreds and thousands, even sometimes ten thousand at once walking in order, having at their head some Priests with *crosses* and *banners*. They often ran with great crowds into the *churches*,

People were so busy performing all kinds of good works, as if they feared that fire would descend from heaven upon the sinners, or that the earth would tear asunder. The wisest people were amazed at such a sudden repentance <note>original: "boedvaardigheid"</note>, and did not know what they should think of it. The *Pope* had not commanded or established it; no *Preacher* had moved the people to it through his eloquence; no person renowned for Holiness had given cause for it. A group of simple people had started it, and these simple people had gained such a following, even of learned and prominent people.

They lashed themselves twice a day, which they did thirty-three times in succession, in memory of the 33 years that *Christ*, according to the general opinion, spent on earth: and while lashing themselves they sang various songs about the death and the suffering of the *Savior*. They confessed to one another back and forth, and gave each other absolution <note>original: "ontbinding" — the formal release from the guilt of sin</note>, although they were nothing but laymen; they were also said to have claimed that their acts of penance were useful and beneficial to the deceased—even to the damned in hell and the blessed in Heaven. only one Sacrament remained: *Scourging* <note>original: "geeffeling," the practice of ritual self-flogging as penance.</note> had taken the place of *Baptism*, and no one could be saved without *scourging* themselves: *The Sacrament of the Altar was not the Lord’s Body*, but the *Cuckoo of the Priests* <note>This was a derogatory term used by the sect to mock the Eucharist, likely suggesting it was a hollow deception or a parasitic invention of the clergy.</note>. *Confession* and *Absolution* <note>The formal process of a priest forgiving sins.</note> were of no use; everything had to be settled through *scourging*; *Elijah* and *Enoch* <note>Two biblical figures who, according to tradition, did not die but were taken to heaven, and were expected to return before the Last Judgment.</note> had appeared in the world long ago: *Elijah* had been burned at *Erfurt* forty years prior; *Enoch* was the Teacher *Conrad Schmidt* <note>original: "Conraad Smith," a historical leader of this late Flagellant movement.</note>, who had first preached this doctrine in *Thuringia*: God had created all souls at the same time in the beginning: In the Last Judgment, *Conrad Schmidt*, and not *Jesus Christ*, would preside as *Judge*. They believed no other days should be celebrated except *Sunday*, *Christmas*, and the *Assumption of Our Lady*. Externally, they practiced religion as in the *Roman Church*, observing the *Feasts* and *Fast days*, and honoring the *Images*. But they intended to make up for the rest by *scourging* themselves bravely. They were all condemned to the fire at *Sangerhausen* and burned alive.

*Hermanus of Schildis*, *Johannes de Indagine*, *Jean Gerson*, and several others have written against this sect, and in Paris a detailed account and description of them was printed under the title *History of the Flagellants* <note>original Latin: "Historia Flagellantium"</note>: Additionally, besides those already mentioned, the following writers can be consulted on the matter, such as: *The Monk of Padua in the Chronicle for the year 1260*; *Albert of Strasbourg for the year 1349*; *Nauclerus, Generation 45*; *Gobelinus Persona in the Course of the World, Age 6, chapter 91*; *Bzovius, Continuation of the Annals*; *Sigonius, On the Kingdom of Italy, book 19, and On the Bishops of Bologna, book 3*; *Baronius, Spondanus, etc.*

### CONSCIENCE-PEOPLE
<note>original: "Gewetensluiden," also known by the Latin name "Conscientiarii."</note> a sect established in the previous century, in the year 1673, by a wandering *student* named *Matthias Knutzen* <note>An early modern German radical who is often cited as one of the first known advocates of atheism and rationalism.</note>, from *Germany*—specifically from the Duchy of *Holstein*. He sought to build a following in various places throughout *Germany*, but the group was dispersed shortly thereafter, after the aforementioned *Knutzen* was refuted in *Jena* by the famous *theologian Dr. Musäus* <note>Johannes Musäus (1613–1681), a prominent Lutheran professor at the University of Jena.</note>. His dangerous doctrine ultimately amounted to this: that *Holy Scripture* was not the rule of faith, but rather that knowledge, alongside *Conscience*, was the true and proper *fundamental belief*, which all people carried within themselves as a *Bible*.

### GNOSIMACHI
<note>Greek for "opponents of knowledge."</note> these are heretics in *Christendom* who reject the study of all sciences, because *God* desires nothing but good works.

### GNOSTICS
a well-known name for *Ancient Heretics*, who caused a great stir especially in the second century. Among scholars, there is much debate regarding the origin of the *Gnostics*. As for the views of these *Gnostics*, these five propositions contain the essence of them.

1. They supposed two Deities, one who worked good and one who worked evil, and called them *Aeons* <term>Aeons: In Gnostic systems, these are divine emanations or beings that represent various powers or attributes of the high God.</term>; but since they did not all agree regarding the origin and the order of these *Aeons*, there were various specific opinions among them.

2. They attributed the creation and preservation of this *Universe* to these *Aeons*, or to certain Angels, and not to an *Almighty* God alone.

3. They believed that the *Law of Moses*, the *Prophecies*, and consequently all the Laws were instituted by the Creator of this World, whom they distinguish from the Almighty, or from the *Aeons* together, who constituted a single Deity.

### Church and Heretic History, Part 2, Book 2, Chapter 4.

GREEKS, although these were the first who accepted the teachings of the Gospel following the testimony of the *Apostles*, and though a great multitude of Church Teachers were found among them—such as *Ignatius*, *Origen*, *Clement of Alexandria*, *Eusebius*, *Athanasius*, *Gregory of Nazianzus*, *Basil*, *Chrysostom*, and others—they have nonetheless been much changed by various heresies that arose among them, and have fallen into great errors through the untimely zeal of the *Monks*.

In the beginning, they were of one mind with the Churches of the *East*; later they began to differ in some doctrines, which distinction revealed itself even more when, in the seventh century, the Pope of *Rome* sought to exert authority. This caused a schism <note>The Great Schism, which formally solidified in 1054, though the author here traces its roots to earlier centuries.</note> between the *Greek* and *Latin* Churches to grow more and more, which was further increased in the eighth century by the *iconoclasm* <term>Iconoclasm: Referred to in the Dutch text as the *beeldenstryd* (struggle over images), this was a period of intense conflict within the Church regarding whether religious icons should be venerated or destroyed.</term>. 

They do not acknowledge the Pope as the Head of the Church in any way, as the *Roman Catholics* do, but consider him merely to be a Patriarch of the Latins. They have four Patriarchs among them: that of *Constantinople*, who is the most prominent; that of *Alexandria*; that of *Antioch*; and that of *Jerusalem*, the last of whom is regarded as the least among them.
