### Greek Church of the Heretics <note>The title "GR der Ketteren" (Greek of the Heretics) reflects the 17th-century perspective of the author's source, likely a Roman Catholic or Western European viewpoint that regarded the Eastern Orthodox Church as schismatic or heretical.</note>

During these *Fasts*, they eat all kinds of fish, but no *milk*, nor anything that resembles *meat*, or is derived from it. The third *Fast* they call *of the Holy Virgin* <note>original Greek: τῆς ἁγίας παρθένου (tēs hagias parthenou); this refers to the Dormition Fast, honoring the "falling asleep" or assumption of Mary.</note>, and it begins on the first of *August*, lasting fourteen days. There are also two days during the great *Lent* of *Easter* when they may eat fish: once on the 25th of March, the day of *the Annunciation of Our Lady*, and on *Palm Sunday*.

The fourth *Fast* is *of the Nativity* <note>original Greek: τῶν Χριστογεννῶν (tōn Christogennōn).</note>, or *Advent*, beginning 40 days before *Christmas* and lasting until that day. The third is eight days before the Feast of *St. Michael*. 

Furthermore, all *Greeks* fast on *Wednesdays* and *Fridays*, and the strictest among them also on *Mondays*. # History of Heretics.

**HELICITES**, heretics of the seventh century, who lived a secluded and solitary life, yet taught that religion consisted of *Holy songs* and *Holy dances* with the *Nuns* <note>original: *Klooster-Zusters*</note>, following the example of *Moses* and of *Miriam* <note>The Dutch text uses "Maria," the traditional name for the sister of Moses, known in English as Miriam; this refers to the celebration after crossing the Red Sea in Exodus 15.</note> after the destruction of *Pharaoh*.

**HENRICIANS**, thus named after *Henry*, a *Monk of Toulouse* <note>Also known as Henry of Lausanne, a 12th-century ascetic preacher.</note>, who lived in the 12th century and, around the year 1147, taught the views of *Peter of Bruys* <note>original: *Pieter Bruis*</note>. He was condemned by the *Council of Pisa* and finally delivered to his Bishop bound hand and foot. Some are of the opinion that the *Henricians* received their name not from him, but from Emperor *Henry the Fourth*, whom they supported against the Pope. *Peter of Cluny, Book against the Petrobrusians; St. Bernard, Epistle 238; Baronius, Annals of Christ 1147; Genebrardus in Chron.; Sanderus, Heresy 142; Arnold’s History of the Church and Heretics, 1st part.*

### ILLUMINATI, or ALUMBRADOS <note>The Spanish term *Alumbrados* translates to "the enlightened ones."</note>
Certain Spanish Heretics, who appeared around the year 1575. This Sect became so numerous that one counted near ten thousand of them: But when their leaders were punished in *Cordova* <note>modern-day Córdoba</note> by the *Inquisition*, the group disappeared almost entirely, until it appeared again in great numbers in the diocese of *Seville* in the year 1623. The Bishop *Don Andreas Pacheco*, Inquisitor General of Spain, had seven of the most prominent among them burned, and forced their followers to renounce their errors once more, or to depart from the Kingdom. The edict <note>original: *Plakkaat*</note> issued against them mentions seventy errors, among which these are the principal: *that by means of internal prayer of the soul, and through union with God (of which they boasted), they were in such a state of perfection that they needed neither good works nor the Sacraments; indeed, that they [could commit] the greatest outrages without sin*

### JACOBITES, *Eastern Christians*
So named after a certain *Jacobus* <note>Jacob Baradaeus (c. 500–578), after whom the Syriac Orthodox Church is often called "Jacobite."</note>, born in *Syria*, and a disciple of *Eutyches* and *Dioscorus* <note>Eutyches and Dioscorus were leaders of the Monophysite movement, which taught that Christ had a single divine nature rather than distinct human and divine natures.</note>, whose heresy he promoted so strongly throughout all of *Asia* and *Africa* at the beginning of the 6th century that eventually all the other various sects into which the *Eutychians* were divided united into that of the *Jacobites* in the 7th century. They have a specific Patriarch in *Asia*, who resides at *Caraemit* <note>modern-day Diyarbakır, Turkey</note>, a city in *Mesopotamia*; the one they currently have in *Africa* is the Patriarch of *Alexandria*, who follows the errors of *Dioscorus* along with the *Copts*. Their Patriarch of *Asia* assumes the title of Patriarch of *Antioch*, although there is a *Greek schism* <note>Referring to the Melkite Greek Orthodox Church, which remained in communion with Constantinople.</note> that holds its seat in *Damascus*

[Richard] Simon <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712) was a prominent French biblical critic and historian of Eastern Christian rites.</note> relates concerning the present state of the *Jacobites*. He says that under this name one must generally include all the *Monophysites* <note>From the Greek 'mono' (one) and 'physis' (nature); those who believe Christ has a single divine-human nature.</note> of the *East*, that is, all those who recognize only one nature in *Jesus Christ*, which are the *Armenians*, the *Copts*, and the *Abyssinians* [Ethiopians]. He adds that those who are specifically called *Jacobites* make up a very small number, being no more than 40 families, who mainly live in *Syria* and *Mesopotamia*; there is a distinction among them, because one part is united with the *Roman Church*, and the other always remains separated from it. These latter are not even well united among themselves, having two rival *Patriarchs* who oppose one another, one of whom resides in *Caraemit* <note>The city of Diyarbakır in modern-day Turkey.</note> and the other in *Dersapharan* <note>The Dayro d-Zafaran or "Saffron Monastery" near Mardin, Turkey.</note>. Besides these two *Patriarchs*, there is another who is of the same mind as the *Latins* [Roman Catholics] and lives in *Aleppo*. *Father Sacchini* <note>Francesco Sacchini (1570–1625), the official historian of the Jesuit Order.</note>, a *Jesuit*, has spoken in the history of his order of a negotiation which *Father Christopher Rodriguez*, an envoy of the Pope, had in *Egypt* with the *Copts*, who are *Jacobites*, concerning the union of the two Churches. Furthermore, it appears from this that the most learned of this sect agree with the *Roman Church* and differ only in expressions. They even say that their expressions serve no other purpose than to distinguish them from the *Nestorians* <note>A group that emphasized the distinction between Christ’s divine and human natures, viewed as the theological opposites of the Jacobites.</note>.

[JACOBI]**TES, or PHANTASIASTS**, are certain heretics who arose in *Alexandria* during the reign of Emperor *Justinian* and opposed the Council of *Chalcedon* <note>The Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) established the orthodox doctrine that Christ has two natures, divine and human, in one person.</note>. A certain point of dispute among the Eutychians <note>Followers of Eutyches, who believed Christ's human nature was absorbed by his divine nature.</note> gave rise to this; namely, whether the body of *Christ* had been *corruptible* <note>Subject to decay, hunger, and physical change.</note> or *incorruptible* from the moment of his conception. *Severus* <note>Severus of Antioch, a prominent Monophysite theologian.</note> held that it had been *corruptible*: but *Julian of Halicarnassus* asserted the contrary, claiming that the body could feel neither hunger nor thirst, nor become weary, but that he suffered these and other things only in outward appearance, and not *actually*; for which reason they were called *Phantasiasts* <note>From the Greek word for "appearance" or "phantom." This group is also known as the Aphthartodocetae.</note>. *Evagrius* reports that Emperor *Justinian* was an adherent of these heretics and persecuted the Orthodox; others, however, defend the Emperor in this regard. *Evagrius, Book 4*. *Procopius's Anecdota* <note>The "Secret History" by Procopius of Caesarea.</note>, *Liberatus in his Summary*. *Leontius of Byzantium, On Sects*. *Nicephorus, Book 17*. *Prateolus*, *Spanheim on Section 6*. *Baronius at the year of Christ 835.*

**MANICHAEANS** are heretics <term>Ketters</term> <note>From the Greek word for "choice," used historically to describe groups whose beliefs deviated from established Church doctrine.</note> whose unholy views were brought forth by a certain *Manes*, a Persian of low birth but well-formed and clever of mind; this was the reason that a certain widow, who had bought him as a slave, adopted him as her son, and had him instructed by the *Magi*, or *Wise Men*, in the philosophy of the Persians. # Alphabetical List of Names: MA

...having been excluded from the fellowship of the Church several times, he was finally readmitted once more after he had shown repentance, renounced his errors, and attempted to enlighten his disciples, who were still few in number. *Marcion* assumed, just like *Cerdonius* <note>A Syrian Gnostic teacher who influenced Marcion in Rome</note>, two deities <note>original: *Godbeden*</note>, or two fundamental principles: one good and righteous, and the other unrighteous and evil. The latter was the source of the creation of the world and of the *Law* <note>The Old Testament laws and commandments</note>, while the former was the source of the *Gospel*. Some ancient writers say that *Marcion* allowed for three fundamental principles: one good, being the Father of *Jesus Christ*; one evil, being the Devil; and a third who was between the two and had created the *World*. However, the most ancient writers, who were better informed on the matter, assure us that *Marcion* held no more than two, and it was, according to *Rhodon* <note>An early Christian writer and opponent of Marcionism</note>, one of his disciples who had invented the third.

*Marcion* also denied the resurrection of bodies, though he granted a sort of resurrection to those who embraced his teachings. He further asserted that when the Lord *Jesus* descended into *Hell*, He released from there *Cain*, the *Sodomites*, and all other godless enemies of God the Creator <note>In Marcion's view, these "villains" were actually the ones who recognized the true God, while the biblical heroes were trapped by the "evil" Creator God</note>, but that He left behind the *Patriarchs* <note>original: *Oudvaderen*</note>, the *Prophets*, and all the righteous of the *Old Testament* who were friends of God and His law. It lasted a long time, and from it sprang many other sects during the time of ***Commodus*** <note>Roman Emperor from 180 to 192 AD</note>, as ***Rhodon*** testifies, who formerly wrote against them. ***Emperor Constantine the Great*** gave several orders in the year 326 for the eradication of the ***Marcionites*** and other heresies. ***Theodoret***, Bishop of ***Cyrrhus*** <note>original: *Cyr*</note>, estimated their number at as many as 10,000 in the year 423, as he himself writes. ### MASBOTHENIANS

Heretics, named as such after *Masbotheus*, whom *Hegesippus* <note>An early Christian chronicler of the 2nd century</note> associates with the *Cleobians* <note>An obscure early sect mentioned by ancient writers alongside other Jewish-Christian groups</note>. ## MENNONITES

MENNONITES, so named after *Menno Simons*, the founder of the *Mennonites*, or *Anabaptists* <note>original: *Doopsgezinden*; a Dutch term for those who emphasize adult baptism upon a confession of faith</note>, who have spread throughout the *Netherlands*, and especially in *Holland*. *Menno Simons* lived at the beginning of the 16th century and was born in a village in *Friesland*. He was initially devoted to the *Roman Catholic* religion, but he abandoned it and allowed himself to be baptized again by an Anabaptist <note>original: *Wederdooper*; literally "re-baptizer"</note> named *Ubbo Philips*. Through his writings, which were published in a volume in *Amsterdam* and subsequently reprinted in the year 1681, he gained great respect among his fellow believers, so much so that he is still regarded as their principal teacher today. He was able to explain his thoughts very clearly and fluently, and gained many followers and pupils in *Leeuwarden*, *Groningen*, and *Emden*, as well as in *Westphalia*, *Gelderland*, *Brabant*, *Holland*, along the *Baltic Sea* <note>original: *Oostzee*</note>, and other places. He rejected *infant baptism* <note>original: *Kinderdoop*</note> and insisted strongly on *believer's baptism* <note>original: *Wederdoop*; re-baptism</note>. In other matters of religion, he was, as it is said, very doubtful...

### MESSALIANS, or MASSALIANS,

a sort of Heretics who arose during the reign of *Constans* <note>Constans I (r. 337–350 AD), son of Constantine the Great</note>, around the year 361. They were also named *Euchites*, that is, *Prayers*, and *Fanatics* <term>Fanatics; the original Dutch term *Geestdryvers* (literally "spirit-drivers") refers to those who claim direct divine inspiration, often accompanied by emotional or erratic behavior</term>. They said that Prayer alone was sufficient above all good works, building their opinion on the words of the Son of God, that one must always pray. The founders of this Sect were *Monks* from *Mesopotamia*, who abandoned their work simply to pray, and did not observe even half of the usual discipline of the Monks. They rejected *Fasting* and held the Seals of the Covenant <term>Seals of the Covenant; a theological term for the sacraments, specifically Baptism and the Lord's Supper</term> to be quite indifferent. They said that Prayer alone was powerful enough to ward off all temptations, to drive out the Devil, and to wipe out sin—which Baptism had not done, since it only shaved sin away, just as a razor does hair, without removing the cause of its regrowth. They believed that every person had two Souls, one of which was heavenly and the other devilish, but that the latter had to yield immediately through Prayer. They presented themselves as Prophets, claiming that they saw the Trinity with their physical eyes, and that in order to become like God, they did not sin, not even in thought. They devised hellish deceptions to [mislead] the innocent...

<summary>This page lists historical sources for the study of dissenters and introduces the Messalians, a 4th-century ascetic sect that prioritized constant prayer over sacraments and work.</summary>

### METAMORPHITES
This was the name given in the 16th century to the *Sacramentarians* <term>Sacramentarians; a term often used by Lutherans and Catholics to describe Reformers (like Zwingli) who denied the physical presence of Christ in the Eucharist</term>, because they taught that Christ’s body, upon his Ascension into Heaven, was changed into a completely Divine essence.

### MONARCHIANS
Heretics who rose up in the Church during the Papacy of *Victor* in the year 196. They recognized no more than one Person in the *Holy Trinity* and claimed that the Father had been crucified <note>This specific belief is known as Patripassianism, suggesting the Father suffered as the Son</note>. These errors were introduced by *Praxeas*. *St. Augustine, On Heresies, chapter 41. Baronius, year of Christ 196.*

### MONOTHELITES
or ### MONOTHELETES
Heretics who disturbed the Church in the seventh century and had their origins among the *Eutychians* <term>Eutychians; followers of Eutyches, who believed Christ had only one nature, a fusion of human and divine</term>. They bore this name because they recognized only one will in Christ <note>The name comes from the Greek "monos" (one) and "thelema" (will)</note>. flourished around the year 172, and wished to be regarded as a very holy man, claiming that he also possessed the spirit of prophecy. His strict way of life earned him great esteem among many, through which he gained a large following. Among others who adhered to him were two women, *Priscilla* and *Maximilla*, who presented themselves as *Prophetesses*; however, when their errors and hypocrisy were discovered, they were cast out of the Church. *Asterius Urbanus* reports in the works of *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian often called the "Father of Church History"</note> that both *Montanus* and *Maximilla* ended their lives by a rope <note>i.e., by hanging</note>, although he only had this according to a rumor. In Church discipline, the *Montanists* were very strict, and never wished to readmit those into the fellowship of the Church who had fallen into adultery or other heavy crimes. They even condemned marriage as a form of <term>lewdness</term> <note>original: "boerery"; likely a variation of "boelerij," meaning fornication or carnal lust. The Montanists were famous for their extreme asceticism and rejection of second marriages</note>, kept many *fasting days*, and abstained from certain kinds of food. They held it to be unjust to flee during persecutions or to buy off danger with money, and they were eager to undergo a martyr's death. It is reported by some that they also did not hold an orthodox teaching regarding the *Divine Trinity*, but others excuse them in that regard. It is also alleged that some among them took the blood of a year-old child—whom they had killed with many pricks—and mixed it with flour to bake bread, which they then used in the celebration of the *Holy Supper*.

### N.

**NATURALISTS** are, in a certain sense, those who are named for denying the Article of the *Trinity*, of free will, and of God’s grace, and who believe that they can obtain eternal life without the grace of *Jesus Christ*, provided they only follow their natural understanding <note>The author uses "natural understanding" to refer to human reason independent of divine revelation</note>.

**ORIGENISTS**, ancient heretics of the Gnostic sect and followers of *Epiphanes* <note>A 2nd-century Gnostic thinker, son of Carpocrates</note>, according to *Epiphanius* <note>Bishop of Salamis and author of the *Panarion*, a famous catalog of heresies</note>, who accuses them of condemning marriage and abandoning themselves to all kinds of debauchery and infamies. ### Alphabetische Naamlyst PE

[he] incited a persecution against *Jerome* <note>original: "Hieronymus"; a prominent early Christian scholar known for his translation of the Bible into Latin.</note>, who had been the first to write against him; and having published four books on *free will* at the same time, he attempted to ensnare *Augustine* through trickery. But this great man, whom God had given to the Church to triumph over error, always pursued him and his followers with invincible strength. The *Councils* of *Africa* condemned his views; Popes *Innocent* and *Celestine* excommunicated him, and Emperor *Honorius* banished him and his followers from *Rome* by a solemn *Edict*. He then returned to his homeland <note>Pelagius was born in Britain, though some sources suggest Ireland.</note>, where *Germanus of Auxerre* and *Lupus of Troyes* refuted his errors; and finally, he died miserably in his delusions.

Besides those previously mentioned, he also denied *Original Sin*, saying that it had not come from *Adam* to his descendants through transmission or procreation, but only through imitation <note>The Pelagian view argued that humans are born neutral and only sin by following Adam's bad example, rather than inheriting a corrupted nature.</note>. Furthermore, he claimed that Divine grace was given according to our merits, or was earned by us. The disciples of this Arch-heretic <note>term: "Arch-heretic" (Aartsketter); a title used by contemporary church writers to denote the leader or founder of a major heresy.</note> were condemned at several *Synods*, and subsequently at the *Council of Ephesus*. Their error, which flatters human nature <note>By suggesting humans can achieve goodness through their own efforts.</note>, was widely followed and often renewed later on. *Augustine* was chosen by the *Councils in Africa* to write against these errors, which he did in his books *On the Remission of Sins* <note>original: "de remissione peccatorum"</note>, *On the Grace of Jesus Christ* <note>original: "de gratia Jesu Christi"</note>, *On Original Sin* <note>original: "de peccato originis"</note>, as well as in his treatise against *Julian*. The principal views of *Pelagius*, besides those...

# PE of the Heretics.

[human nature] already mentioned, were: *That Adam had been mortal by nature even before the Fall: That sin is not the cause of death: That our human being comes from God, but our righteousness comes from ourselves: That there are three ways to salvation, namely, the Law of Nature, the Law of Moses, and the Law of Christ: That the works of the Heathens are truly good and pleasing to God, notwithstanding that they are performed without the assistance and help of Divine grace.* He mingled grace with the powers of nature, and by the former he understood only the revealed will of God, along with a certain internal enlightenment of the mind which is given to assist man; yet he nonetheless wished to know nothing of the necessity of prevenient <note>original: "voorkomende"; grace that "comes before" or precedes human effort to incline the will toward God.</note> and cooperating grace to move our heart and our will. He taught, *that peace of mind and justification were caused by our own merits, namely, when we made a right use of free will and applied ourselves to keeping the commandments of God; that thus righteousness and salvation were not given through mere grace or faith in Christ; that the cause of election to grace and glory was the foresight of good works and perseverance in them through a right use of free will, with the sole exception of the grace of Apostleship; that there was also a pre-ordination (Predestination) and election to death, but that God only had foreknowledge of the sin.* <note>Pelagius argued that God knows who will sin but does not actively decree or "predestine" their damnation, emphasizing human choice.</note> He also taught, *that all oaths were wrong, and that the Rich could not be saved.*

The principal writings of Pelagius are 14 Books of commentaries on the Epistles <note>Referring to the Epistles of St. Paul.</note>

### PE of the Heretics.

[Chry]sostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his powerful preaching.</note> speaks of him in one of his letters, in which he laments the fall of the monk *Pelagius*, but it is probable that this was another *monk* of the same name, distinct from the *arch-heretic* <note>original: "Aartsketter"; a term used historically for the founder or leader of a major movement deemed heretical by the Church.</note>, who was not in the *East* at that time, but in *Rome*, where he arrived at the end of the fourth century. The priest *Rufinus* (whether it was the famous *Rufinus of Aquileia* <note>A monk and historian known for translating Greek patristic works into Latin.</note> or another) joined him in friendship and in doctrine. He then began (around the year 400) to teach his errors within *Rome*. One can categorize his heretical errors into three main headings:

> (1) *That man can turn himself toward the good without the help of grace, and that grace is given in proportion to how much one has earned it.* (2) *That man can reach a state of perfection in which he is no longer subject to the passions or to sin.* (3) *That there is no original sin <note>original: "oorspronkelyke of Erfzonde"</note>, and that children who die without baptism are not damned.*

*Caelestius* was a student of *Pelagius* in *Rome*, and departed from there with him in the year 409. They retreated to *Sicily*, where they stayed for some time, and from there they traveled to *Africa* in the year 411. But *Pelagius* did not remain there long, and went to *Palestine*, where he was well received by *John of Jerusalem*, an enemy of *Jerome* <note>original: "Hieronymus"; Saint Jerome, best known for his translation of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note>. He was pointed out to this Bishop by *Orosius* <note>Paulus Orosius, a historian and theologian who was a student of Augustine.</note>, and there was a negotiation in the year 415 between *Orosius* and *Pelagius*, the conclusion of which was that a delegation would be sent to Pope *Innocent* <note>Pope Innocent I, who eventually condemned Pelagianism.</note> to judge the dispute.

### Alphabetical Name List PE

Two Bishops from *Provence*, *Hero*, Archbishop of *Arles*, and *Lazarus* of *Aix*, who were then in *Palestine*, brought this matter before a Council of 14 Bishops held at *Diospolis* <note>Modern-day Lod in Israel; the council took place in 415 AD.</note>. *Pelagius* appeared there, and after having recanted a portion of his errors, he was acquitted. Meanwhile, the Bishops of *Africa*, who had condemned *Caelestius*, wrote forcefully to *Rome* against *Pelagius*. Since Pope *Innocent* <note>Pope Innocent I, who served as Bishop of Rome from 401 to 417.</note> had died by the time their letters arrived, his successor *Zosimus* initially favored *Pelagius* and *Caelestius*; however, he subsequently abandoned them and condemned their errors. *Pelagius* and his followers were driven out of *Rome* and out of *Italy* following an *Edict* from the Emperor *Honorius*, issued at *Ravenna* on April 30th in the year 418. Meanwhile, the heresy of *Pelagius* established itself in the *West* and in the *East*. *Atticus*, Bishop of *Constantinople*, rejected their representatives; they were driven out of *Ephesus*, and *Theodore*, Bishop of *Antioch*, condemned them and expelled *Pelagius*, who had returned to *Palestine*. But it is not known what became of him after that, and he is mentioned no more in the histories. He wrote a treatise on the *Trinity*; a commentary on the letters of *Paul*; a *Book on the Way to Live Well*; various letters, among which was the one addressed to the Virgin *Demetrias* (which is found among the works of *Jerome* <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note>), several writings in his own defense, and four books on free will. *Augustine, Against Heresies, 88* <note>original Latin: "Augustin. contra haeres. 88"; a reference to Saint Augustine's catalog of 88 heresies, where Pelagianism is the final entry.</note>.

**PEPUZIANS**, certain heretics who emerged from the Montanists <note>A prophetic movement in early Christianity named after its founder, Montanus.</note>, whose errors they followed. They derived their name from a small town in *Phrygia* <note>An ancient region in central Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note> called *Pepuza*, to which they wanted people to gather from all sides. Among them, women held Episcopal <note>The office of a Bishop.</note> and Priestly dignities. They appeared in the second century. *Epiphanius, On Heresies, 49. Augustine, On Heresies, chapter 27. Eusebius, book 5 of History. Baronius. Year of Christ 173.*

**PHILADELPHIAN SOCIETY**, is a company of certain people who are nowadays given the name of *Pietists* <note>A movement within Lutheranism emphasizing individual piety and a "living faith."</note>, who hold private meetings and, among other things, hope for a millennial kingdom <note>original: "duizend jaarig Ryk"; the belief that Christ will reign on earth for a thousand years.</note> which will consist of a glorious state of the Church. They further claim that the inward Spirit of God teaches everything, and that one must pay heed to it. In the year 1704, this name of the *Philadelphian Society* also became known in London, England, whose principal members were *Jane Lead* <note>original: "Jean Leade," an English mystic (1624–1704).</note> and *John Pordage* <note>original: "Jehu Pordage," an English physician and mystic.</note>, a physician, from where this name afterwards spread to Germany.

# Alphabetical Name List PI

...made himself known through several heretical propositions. He was *Bishop* of *Sirmium* <note>An important city in the Roman province of Pannonia, modern-day Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia.</note>, and governed that Church for a long time without allowing any of his views to appear; finally, he revealed himself and sought to maintain that no *pre-existence* or *Divinity* could be attributed to *Christ* before his birth from *Mary*. *The Word*, of which one reads in the Evangelist *John*, he distinguished from the man *Christ*; the former he regarded as *eternal*; but *Jesus*, whom he viewed as a mere man, he would not recognize as eternal. He was otherwise learned and eloquent. *Cave, Literary History, page 113.*

### *PICARDS*,

this is the name given to the followers of a certain man who, around the beginning of the 15th century, surpassed the error of the *Adamites* <note>A sect that practiced religious nudity, claiming to have returned to Adam's state of innocence.</note> regarding nudity; his name was *Picard*, and he traveled from *Flanders* to *Germany*, and penetrated as far as *Bohemia*. It has been said that he deceived people through *sorcery* <note>original: "beguigelinge"; referring to deceptive magic or delusions.</note>. This much is certain, that in a short time he had a large number of followers, both men and women. He commanded them to always go naked, which was more than the *Adamites* mentioned by *Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Salamis known for his "Panarion," a massive compilation of heresies.</note> did, who contented themselves with stripping naked only in their assemblies. He called himself a <note>The text likely continues "Son of God" on the next page, as indicated by the catchword "Zoone" (Son).</note>

### PRE-ADAMITES

**PRE-ADAMITES**, thus are named people who are alleged to have existed before the creation of *Adam*, or also those who have believed that such people existed. Those who believe that the World is eternal and has been renewed several times, claim that there were formerly people before *Adam*, and one even finds this sentiment among some **Church Fathers** <note>The influential early Christian theologians whose writings established the intellectual foundations of Christianity.</note>. For example, **St. Clement of Alexandria** in his book named *Hypotyposeis* <note>original: "Hupotypofis"; a lost work titled "Outlines" or "Sketches."</note>, believed in eternal matter, the **transmigration of souls** <term>transmigration of souls: the philosophical or religious concept that the soul, after biological death, begins a new life in a new body</term>, and that there had been several Worlds before *Adam*. **Julian the Apostate** <note>The Roman Emperor (r. 361–363) who rejected Christianity in favor of Neoplatonic Hellenism.</note> was of the opinion that in the beginning several people were created, and those are also the thoughts of various **Mohammedans** <note>An archaic term for Muslims.</note>. The Author of the book *Kuzari* <note>original: "Cozai"; referring to the work by the Jewish philosopher Judah Halevi.</note> speaks of some ancient monuments in which he mentions *Janbuzar*, *Zagrit*, and *Roana*, who had lived before *Adam*. ### Principles of the Heretics.

Egyptians, it is true, have believed themselves to be the first people of the world, but it is easy to see that their alleged origin is mythical. Their historians say that there were kings among them during a period of thirty-six thousand five hundred and twenty-five years, up until *Nectanebo* <note>original: "Nectanebus"; Nectanebo II (reigned 360–342 BC), the last native pharaoh of ancient Egypt.</note>, who was driven from the throne by *Ochus* <note>Artaxerxes III Ochus, the King of Persia.</note>, King of the *Persians*, nineteen years before the Monarchy of *Alexander the Great*. They say that the Gods, and Heroes, or demigods, ruled in this Kingdom during a period of thirty-five thousand two hundred and one years, and that they were followed by the Kings, of whom *Menes* <note>Traditionally considered the first human king of Egypt and the founder of the First Dynasty.</note> was the first. The famous *Manetho* <note>original: "Manethon"; an Egyptian priest and historian (3rd century BC) whose chronology is still used as a framework for Egyptian history.</note>, Priest of the City of *Heliopolis*, who wrote the History of *Egypt* by order of King *Ptolemy Philadelphus* <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus (reigned 283–246 BC), a great patron of scholarship and the Library of Alexandria.</note>, following this ancient Chronicle, has the Gods and Heroes rule over the lands of the Nile; but he does not count such a great number of them, nor does he grant them so many years of reign. It is evident that this reign of the Gods and demigods is nothing other than fictions invented by the Egyptians to rival the antiquity of the *Chaldeans*; these two nations always envied one another in this matter, and attributed to themselves Princes or astronomical observations that extended very far before their actual origin. *Diodorus* <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note> therefore says of the *Egyptians* that they have forsaken the truth to follow wonderful and unbelievable lies. Finally, something must be said of the Antiquity of the *Chi-* <note>The text cuts off here as it moves to the next page.</note>

The consequence of the execution of this severe sentence against *Priscillianus* was that it caused a great deal of disorder; for the punishment of this Arch-heretic <note>original: "Aartsketter"; a term used for the founder or primary leader of a heretical sect.</note> only served to strengthen his heresy. # QU of the Heretics.

**QUIETISTS** was the name given in the Greek Church in the 14th century to certain persons who boasted of a singular tranquility of mind, which they partook in during prayer. For this reason, they were also called *Hesychastae* <note>original: *Heſychaſtæ*, from the Greek word for "stillness" or "quiet"</note> in the Greek language, which means as much as **Quietists**. The principal founder and leader of these people was **Simeon** <note>likely referring to Symeon the New Theologian, whose mystical writings influenced the later movement</note>, Abbot of a monastery by **Mount Athos**, who was held in great esteem by his followers. Joined with him was also **Gregorius Palamas**, who eventually became the Bishop of **Thessalonica**, and was a learned and eloquent man. On the contrary, **Barlaam**, a monk of the Order of **Basilius** <note>St. Basil</note>, opposed him with great vehemence; he made use of the simplicity of some monks who were devoted to this sect to discover their secrets, and thereupon began to reproach them with all kinds of follies and erroneous sentiments.

Among these [accusations] was especially that they were said to have claimed that, through a certain posture of the body, they saw remarkable things—namely, when *they bowed the head to the chest and toward the navel, held their breath, and looked at the navel with unswerving eyes until they found the heart and the powers of the Soul within, thus they were filled with a Divine light, blew out the fire of the Holy Spirit through the nose, and had the most pleasant feeling;* just as they were therefore called *Omphalopsychi* <note>Greek: "navel-souls"</note> or *Umbilicanimi* <note>Latin: "navel-souls"</note> by **Barlaam**. ## SABATHIANS

SABATHIANS, Heretics among the Christians, named after a baptized Jew called *Sabathius*. He moved the *Easter Festival* to the 14th of March, held secret meetings, and mixed Jewish customs into the Christian religion; he sought only to progress far enough that he would be appointed Bishop by his followers.

## SABELLIANS

SABELLIANS were certain Heretics in the 3rd century who took their name from their founder, *Sabellius*. He was a native of *Pentapolis* in *Libya* and had been a student of the Heretic *Noëtius*. The same errors are attributed to him, so much so that *Augustine*, *Epiphanius*, and *Philastrius* <note>Three major Church Fathers known for documenting and refuting heresies.</note> were not satisfied with the fact that these two <note>Sabellius and Noëtius.</note> had been categorized as distinct sects. This *Sabellius* was initially orthodox but left the Church in the year 257, as he taught *that God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were but one Person, just as the Soul, Spirit, and Body in us make up only one man*; indeed, it is added...

Whether he died in that same year is uncertain. His followers were called *Unionites*, *Monarchists*, and *Patropassians*, or *Father-sufferers*. The first name was given to them because, like Sabellius, they made only one Person out of the three Divine Persons; the second, because they taught that without this view the Divine Dominion <note>original: *Monarchia*; referring to the absolute unity of God.</note> could not exist; and the third, because they maintained that God the Father had taken on flesh and suffered <note>From the Latin *pater* (father) and *passio* (suffering).</note>. *Roscellinus* <note>A 12th-century philosopher and theologian often accused of Sabellianism.</note> revived the heresy of Sabellius. *Epiphanius, Heresies 57 & 60. **SACCOPHORI**, a certain sect among the *Messalian Heretics* <note>An ascetic group from the 4th century who believed that intense prayer was the only way to expel the demon that they believed every person possessed from birth.</note>, who received their name because they used to cover themselves with coarse sacks <note>The name comes from the Greek *sakkos*, meaning sackcloth, used as a sign of penance or humility.</note>.

**SELEUCIANS** were heretics, originating from *Seleucus* and *Hermias*, in the 4th century. They claimed God was *corporeal* <note>Attributing a physical, material body to God rather than seeing the Divine as pure spirit.</note> and maintained that the primary matter [of the universe] was *eternal*. They branded those whom they baptized with a hot iron on the forehead and held other errors that conflicted with the honor of the *Word* <note>Referring to the "Logos," or Jesus Christ.</note> that became *flesh*. *St. Augustine, Heresies 59. Nicephorus, book 2, chapter 14. Philastrius, Sanderus, Prateolus.*

**SEMI-ARIANS**, heretics who did not exactly claim with *Arius* <note>Arius taught that Jesus was a created being, not equal to God the Father.</note> that the *Son* is unlike the *Father*, but would not accept the word *Consubstantial* <note>original: *Consubstantialis*; meaning "of one and the same substance." This was the defining term of the Nicene Creed.</note> or *of the same essence*, but for the rest admitted that he was of like essence <note>original: *gelijkwezig*; this middle-ground position is often called "Homoiousian," meaning "of similar substance" rather than "of the same substance."</note> with the *Father*.

**SEMI-PELAGIANS**, heretics who arose in *France* <note>Specifically the region of Gaul.</note> in the 5th century; they rejected *Augustine's* views on *Grace* and *Predestination* and attributed much to *Free Will*. *Cassian* <note>John Cassian, a monk whose writings on spiritual discipline were highly influential despite these theological disputes.</note> is also counted among this sect. *Prosper* <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a staunch defender of Augustine’s theology.</note> gave a report on these people to *Augustine*, who was thereby moved to write the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* <note>original: *de Praedestinatione Sanctorum*</note> and *On the Gift of Perseverance* <note>original: *de dono perseverantiae*</note> against them.

The actual founder of this teaching was *Michael Servetus*, who was a Spaniard by birth and a physician by profession, and was burned [at the stake] in Geneva in the year 1553. <note>Servetus was executed for heresy during the Reformation, a pivotal moment in history that remains controversial due to John Calvin's role in the trial.</note> Since the year 1523, he had expanded his errors both in writing and orally, especially in *Italy*, and won over the minds of many there—so much so that around the year 1546, over forty people were found in the territory of *Venice* who held secret meetings and conversations aimed at overthrowing the doctrine of the *Holy Trinity* and the <term>atonement</term> <note>original: "voldoening" - referring to the theological concept of Christ's death satisfying divine justice.</note> of *Christ*. Among these were *Laelius Socinus*, *Bernardino Ochino*, *Nicolaus Paruta*, *Valentinus Gentilis*, *Julius Trevisanus*, *Franciscus de Ruego*, *Jacobus de Chiari*, *Franciscus Niger*, *Faustus Socinus*, *Paulus Alciatus*, and others. However, as soon as this was discovered, some were handed over for proper punishment, and the others were scattered, spreading themselves here and there and further extending their poison. <note>The author uses "poison" as a common historical metaphor for perceived heresy.</note> *Laelius Socinus* was one of the most prominent, who made a journey through *Switzerland*, *France*, *England*, the Netherlands, Germany, and *Poland*, promoting his errors wherever he could. Consequently, several people were found here and there, especially in *Poland*, who were very inclined toward these views. Regarding *Poland*, much was contributed by *Giorgio Blandrata*, who was also a student of Servetus and a physician by profession—serving as the personal physician to the King of Poland—and was held in great esteem by many,

After *Lelius Socinus* died in *Zurich* in the year 1562, his brother’s son *Faustus Socinus* followed in his footsteps after some time, through which the followers of this teaching increased so much that they received the name *Socinians* from it. But one must not forget to add that they were initially granted two years to remain in the Kingdom to put their affairs in order, so that the date of their departure was first set for July 10, 1660. During these two years, they were subjected to all kinds of mistreatment; they could only sell their property at a very low price, and they encountered obstacles everywhere despite all the treaties and solemn oaths of the Kings under whose shadow they had lived for a century, including *John Casimir* <note>John II Casimir Vasa, King of Poland, who signed the decree of banishment in 1658.</note>...

**SOCINUS (FAUSTUS)**, nephew of Lælius Socinus; his father was Alexander, son of Marianus Socinus the Younger; his mother was Agnes Petrucci, daughter of Borgesius Petrucci and Victoria Piccolomini. Our Faustus expanded the errors of his uncle with such great diligence that the Socinians, as it is said, primarily received their name from him. He was born in Siena <note>A city in Tuscany, Italy.</note> on December 5th of the year 1539. In addition to this, through his kinship—and especially through the letters of Lælius Socinus—the latter's errors were instilled in him at an early age. Following this, he went to *Italy*, and stayed for a time at the Court of *Florence*, where he was held in reasonable esteem by the Grand Duke and remained for twelve years, seeming no longer to concern himself with the new sentiments of his Uncle. Finally, he had a change of heart, voluntarily left this way of life, and in the year 1574 came to *Germany*, refusing to return even though the Grand Duke urged him to do so. In the year 1578, he held a dispute at *Zurich* against *Francois Pucci*, and when in *Transylvania* <term>Transylvania</term> <note>original: "Zevenbergen"; a historical region now in modern-day Romania where the Unitarian Church was legally recognized.</note> the conflict between *Francis David* <note>original: "Frans Davidson"; a leading figure in the Hungarian Unitarian Church who eventually rejected the prayer to Christ.</note> and *Giorgio Biandrata* <note>original: "George Blandrata"; an Italian physician and influential leader of the anti-Trinitarians in Poland and Transylvania.</note> arose regarding the adoration of *Christ*, *Socinus* was summoned there to settle the matter. **SOCINUS (LÆLIUS)** was the son of *Marianus Socinus*, whom one must call "the Younger" to distinguish him from another *Marianus*, his grandfather. However, after these gatherings were discovered and the authorities intended to punish those who attended them accordingly, *Socinus*, along with several others, escaped punishment by fleeing. ### SUPRALAPSARIANS, ANTELAPSARIANS
<note>Theological terms from the Latin "supra" (before) and "lapsus" (the fall).</note> After the beginning of the 17th century, those in the Reformed Church were so named by their opponents who claimed that God, clearly before the creation of Adam and without any regard for his fall, had chosen some people for eternal life and some for eternal death, because as an absolute Lord He could deal with His creatures according to His pleasure. To these, the *Infralapsarians* <note>Those who believed God's decree of election happened with the "fall" of humanity in view.</note> were opposed.

### SYNCRETISTS
This is the name given to those who seek to unite various religions with one another, or at least who wish to establish peace, harmony, and friendship among those who hold different opinions in religious matters, or at least in what concerns the foundations of faith. # SY [Syncretists] of the Heretics.

...are called by those who have sought to bring the clashing *philosophers* <term>Wyſgeeren: philosophers or seekers of wisdom</term> into agreement with one another; however, according to the meaning of this word, those are understood by it who undertake this in matters of religion. The origin of this name is derived from the *Cretans* <term>Cretenfers: inhabitants of the island of Crete</term>, who, although they were at odds among themselves, nevertheless, whenever foreign enemies appeared, immediately reconciled with each other and opposed them with armed hand; yet this lasted no longer than the war with the foreigners lasted, and as soon as this had an end, their differences began anew, which were never fundamentally uprooted. Therefore, those who have sought a union among various religions, without one or the other party completely abandoning its opinion, have now been called *Syncretists* <note>From the Greek "synkretismos," originally referring to a federation of Cretan cities; in theology, it refers to the blending of different, often conflicting, beliefs.</note>. When a city was conquered, he handed it over to his people for plundering, with only the "cobwebs in the chimneys"—by which he meant sausages and hams—excepted <note>Žižka famously prioritized securing food supplies for his troops over traditional loot.</note>. He was born in *Egypt*, an eloquent man, and a follower of *Platonic Philosophy*. It is alleged that because someone else was preferred over him for a certain Bishopric, this led him to fall away from the *Orthodox* <note>In this historical context, "Orthodox" refers to the mainstream, proto-orthodox Christian church before the major denominational splits.</note> faith and arrive at the delusions of the 30 Gods, which he called *Aeons* <note>original: "Æones"; from the Greek 'aion', meaning 'eternity'. His listeners also adhered to the errors of the *Gnostics*, and called themselves by their name. *Valentinus* published a Gospel and *Psalms*. He came to *Rome* and renounced his errors; but it was not to last: for afterwards he began to defend them anew, indeed with greater zeal than before. ### W.

**Waldensians**, regarding the origin, the name, and the teachings of the *Waldensians*, these were discussed above in the Article on their Brothers, the *Albigensians* <note>A medieval religious movement in Southern France; like the Waldensians, they were often persecuted by the Catholic Church.</note>, on page 13. *Peter Waldo* <note>original: "Petrus Waldus"</note>, one of their most prominent proponents, and from whom some derive their name, was a wealthy Merchant in *Lyons*, who according to some lived in the seventh century, according to others in the eleventh, or as most say in the twelfth century, around the year 1170. Thereupon he began to read the Bible diligently and to explain it to his household, and afterwards to others who came to him in great numbers. He also translated the Bible into the French language and had copies made of it for anyone who wanted them. This soon became public knowledge and set the clergy in arms <note>original: "tegen hem in 't harnafſch"; a Dutch idiom meaning to provoke someone to fierce opposition or "to put them in their armor."</note> against him; but notwithstanding this, he gained a very large following. **ANABAPTISTS, REBAPTIZERS,**
are people who appeared primarily in the 16th century during the time of *Luther’s Reformation* in *Münster* <note>Referring to the Münster Rebellion (1534–1535), where radical Anabaptists took control of the city before being violently suppressed.</note>; they reject *Infant Baptism* and instead require *Re-baptism* of those who convert to them from the *Roman* religion. They teach that Christ did *not* take his flesh in his mother’s body from her essence <note>A specific theological doctrine known as "celestial flesh," suggesting Jesus did not inherit human nature from Mary.</note>. They also do not allow the *Swearing of Oaths* and they reject *Civil Authority*. Furthermore, they claimed a *Monarchy* among themselves over other people, and were very fond of *Polygamy* and the community of goods. In *Holland*, the *Baptist-minded* are also called *Mennonites* (a), though in their published *Confession* they nevertheless recognize the *Civil Authority* as an ordinance of God, and they detest *Polygamy*; they also possess their own property and engage in trade. The *Lords States General* <note>The sovereign governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note> obtained a *General Amnesty* in the year 1711, through their *Minister* in *Bern*, *Switzerland*, for all *Mennonites* imprisoned and oppressed in the *Canton of Bern*. The aforementioned government allowed them to sell their goods and depart for other *Lands*, on the condition that they would never again enter the *Bernese* territory.

### WYCLIFFITES

**WYCLIFFITES**, so named after *John Wycliffe*, born in *Loughborough* in *Leicestershire*, placed among the heretics by the Roman Catholics. He was considered by everyone in his time to be an excellent philosopher and theologian, and was highly esteemed for his singular piety. He taught Holy Theology publicly with great renown at *Oxford*, and was later the rector of the church at *Lutterworth* in the province of *Leicester*. He applied himself not only to the

The *Protestants* say therefore that only the bad state of the *Roman Church* gave *Wycliffe* the occasion for the *Reformation*, and that it is consequently groundless what is claimed by some, namely, that he did it out of spite because they would not make him a *Bishop*. His positions mostly agree with those of the *Protestants*; which is why he, like them, had to suffer a great deal. Since this Bull begins with the words "The Only-Begotten Son of God" <note>Latin: "Unigenitus Dei Filius"</note>, it is commonly called the Constitution Unigenitus. When it arrived in France, the Cardinal and Archbishop of Paris, the Duke of Noailles, refused to proclaim it before he had consulted with the clergy about it. Several conferences were held because of this, but it was claimed that it conflicted with the liberty of the Gallican Church <note>The Gallican Church refers to the Roman Catholic Church in France, which traditionally maintained a degree of independence from the Pope’s administrative and political control</note> if Papal Bulls were accepted so blindly without first being examined by the clergy. Because the infallibility of the Pope suffered a great blow through this, and the Pope also strongly insisted on its acceptance, and the former King Louis XIV absolutely demanded the same of the clergy—though the Archbishop of Paris and his followers opposed it to the utmost—a great upheaval arose in France regarding this Constitution. The most prominent prelates and clergy, especially after the death of Louis XIV, went over to Cardinal de Noailles; indeed, on April 7, 1717, they even appealed to a general National Council. Among these were primarily the four so-called "Appealing Bishops" <note>Original: "appeleerende Bisschoppen"</note> of Mirepoix, Montpellier, Senez, and Boulogne, and neither the Papal nor the French Court could find any means to settle this confused matter. *...to avoid greater unrest, on October 7, 1717, a Royal Edict was issued, stating that the disputes regarding this Bull <note>The Bull Unigenitus</note> should remain suspended and be buried in eternal silence; furthermore, no one was to speak, write, print, or sell anything further regarding this matter until His Holiness <note>The Pope</note> had found a means to completely remove these differences. Anyone who acted against this in the meantime would be regarded as a rebel and a disturber of the common peace.*

But even by this means, it was in no way possible to prevent both parties—namely the Appellants <note>Those who appealed the Papal Bull to a General Council</note> and the Non-Appellants—from fiercely persecuting one another until now. In March 1720, the Regent <note>Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, who governed France during the minority of Louis XV</note> gained hope of resolving the matter through a compromise, since a certain "body of doctrine" <note>Original: "ligbaam der leere," referring to the *Corps de Doctrine*, a document intended to clarify the controversial Bull</note> had been drafted, according to which the Constitution <note>The Bull Unigenitus</note> would be explained and accepted. Some entered into such a compromise, among whom was Cardinal de Noailles, but others restricted themselves to the "body of doctrine" without accepting the Constitution; others remained attached solely to their Appeal and renewed it, as the matter had already been placed before the Tribunal of the Church; and still others insisted that the Constitution must be accepted purely and simply. Although the Regent urged that this compromise be registered and proclaimed in the High Council, the Pope was nevertheless not satisfied with it. Furthermore, even more factions have arisen in France because of it, and spirits have been embittered rather than united.

This does not mean, however, that these monks always performed the service without sleeping; for that is impossible, but they divided their community into several <term>Choirs</term> <note>original: *Choren*</note>, and each of them sang the same service one after another: so that, while resting in turns, they occupied themselves with singing God’s praise through all hours of the night, one after the other. This institution of monks, whose monasteries echoed without ceasing with the praise of God, passed from the East to the West. It was in use in the monasteries of the *Roman Church*. *Sigismund*, King of *Burgundy*, introduced this into the monastery of *Agaune*; King *Dagobert* into that of *St. Denis*; and King *Gontran* into that of *St. Benignus of Dijon*. One also sees that in early times, the Greeks made use of them, as they did other clerics, to carry their letters, but that was not a duty particularly unique to them. ### Appendix of the AC

...of the priestly garments. They were called *Acolytes*, because they served those who performed the [sacred] service. There were in the *Roman Church* three kinds of *Acolytes*: those of the *Palace* <note>original: *Palijs*</note>, who served the *Pope*; the *Stationary* (*Stationarii*) <note>Clergy assigned to specific churches where the Pope held "station" services</note> who served in the *Churches*; and the *Regional* (*Regionarii*) who assisted the *Deacons* in the services they performed in the various districts of *Rome*. At present, the duty of the *Acolytes* is to carry the *Candlesticks* with lit *wax candles* for the service, and in the same manner to accompany the *Deacon* when he goes to sing the *Gospel*. In former times, the *Canons* of the *Cathedrals* were divided into four orders, namely the *Priests*, the *Deacons*, the *Subdeacons*, and the *Acolytes*; each of these orders had its head, and that of the latter was called the *Arch-Acolyte*. This official did not appear in the choir and had no vote in the <term>Chapter</term> <note>The governing body of a cathedral or collegiate church</note>, any more than the other *Acolytes*; however, this rank has now been abolished.

This name is also sometimes used in another sense. The Emperors of *Constantinople* had attendants whom they called *Acolytes*. In Greek ecclesiastical customs, the name <note>original: Ἀκολουθία, *Akólouthia*</note> <note>Meaning "sequence" or "following"</note> is given to the sequence of the service, and to the ceremonies of the other *Sacraments* and *Prayers*. The name of *Acolytes* was also given to those who would not desist from the resolution they had taken; and for this reason, the same name was given to the *Stoic Philosophers*, because they never changed their opinion and even believed that it was a cowardice to do so.

### AGAPETÆ, AGAPETES
was the name given to those *Virgins* who lived in community with one another; but later, the name was applied to those *Daughters* <note>In this context, "daughters" refers to unmarried women or virgins</note> who lived in the homes of the *Clergy*. From this, a great abuse subsequently arose, as the Clergy entered into carnal relations with them, while pretending that they nonetheless remained virgins. These so-called daughters were called *Agapetes*, which is to say, *Worthy* or *Beloved*, through a poor imitation of the Apostle *John*, who addresses *Gaius* in this manner in his third Epistle. They were also called <term>syneisaktous</term> <note>original: συνεισάκτους</note>, or *Introduced ones*, because they entered into the chambers and the beds of their "brothers"—for that is what they called the men with whom they lived. This abuse was strictly forbidden at the Council of Nicaea; just as *Chrysostom* and *Jerome* also campaigned powerfully against it. The name *Agapetes* was also given to the Clergy themselves who associated with these women or daughters in such a manner. See Beveridge in *Notes on the Pandects*, page 45; Valesius in *Eusebius’ Ecclesiastical History*, book 7, chapter 30; Arnold’s *Portrait of the First Christians*; Sanderus, *Heresy 79*; and Prateolus under the word *Agapetes*.

### POVERTY
among the Catholic <term>Mendicant Orders</term> <note>Religious orders that originally relied on charity and owned no property, such as the Franciscans or Dominicans.</note> is divided into the *Great*, *Greater*, and *Greatest*. The *Great Poverty* consists in this: that a monastery may indeed possess some fixed assets <note>Real estate or land.</note>, but no more than is necessary for their subsistence; with this the *Carmelites* and *Augustinians* are content. The *Greater Poverty* consists in this: that a monastery may possess no fixed assets, but may own movable objects, such as books, clothing, provisions of food and drink, rents, and similar things; to which the *Dominicans* have bound themselves. The *Greatest Poverty* consists in this: that a monastery may own nothing at all, neither movable nor immovable assets; which the *Franciscans*, and among them especially the *Capuchins*, adopt.

### AUGUSTINIAN MONKS
bear this name because Pope *Alexander IV*, in the year 1256, imposed upon them the rule that is attributed to *St. Augustine*.

### ORDER OF SAINT BASIL

ORDER OF SAINT BASIL, thus named after *Basil*, Bishop of *Caesarea*, who was greatly persecuted by the *Arians* <note>Followers of Arianism, a belief that Christ was not co-eternal with God the Father, which was declared heretical at the Council of Nicaea.</note> and other *heretics*, yet he bravely resisted them and defended the truth of the *Christian Religion* against *Eustathius*, an *Arian Bishop* at *Sebaste*, as well as against *Apollinaris*; he also labored for the union of the *Eastern* and *Western Churches*, which were divided at that time. He decided around the year 357 to lead a lonely, secluded life, and for those who followed him, he prescribed certain *Rules*, which *Cardinal Bessarion* <note>A 15th-century scholar and cardinal who worked to preserve Greek knowledge in the West.</note>, being devoted to that order, condensed into 25 Articles in the 15th century. This order is one of the oldest and has spread mostly in the East, just as today almost all *Eastern Monks* are devoted to it. In

### BENEDICTINES

BENEDICTINES are Monks who follow the Rule of *St. Benedict*, after whom their order is called the *Benedictine Order*.

This order of *Benedict* has made itself so famous in the *West* that it did there what the Order of *Basil* did in the *East*: that is, it brought all the rules under a single rule, and it united all the other Orders to form just one single Order. The *Benedictine Order* remained in this unity for a long time, but having fallen into irregularity, several reforms were necessary to restore it. Some of these reforms have changed neither the habit <note>The traditional clothing or robe of a monk.</note> nor the name of the Order of *Benedict*, although they have formed various brotherhoods; others have changed in name and habit, even though they originated from the Order of *Benedict*.

One cannot sufficiently measure the great services that the *Christian Religion* has received from this Order for nearly 1,200 years. A large part of the world is indebted to them for the abandonment of *Idolatry* <note>The worship of idols or false gods.</note>, and the

The *Benedictine Monks* wear a wide black robe, with large and wide sleeves, as well as a hood that covers their head, but tapers to a point at the top and hangs on their back.

Their Founder, *St. Benedict*, lived in the sixth century. From this order, several others subsequently emerged, such as the *Carthusians*, the *Camaldolese*, *Celestinians*, *Sylvestrines*, the *Bursfelde Union* <note>original: "Bursfelder Unie"; a 15th-century reform movement of Benedictine monasteries in Germany.</note>, and others.

**BENEDICTINE NUNS** are those who follow the Rule of *St. Benedict*. They wear a black robe with a black scapular <note>A garment consisting of a long piece of cloth worn over the shoulders.</note>, and over that an outer garment with large sleeves of the same color; they also have a round neck-cloth and a black head-veil. These are also divided into several types.

**BERNARDINE MONKS** were founded by *Robert*, Abbot of *Molesme* <note>The OCR reads "Molerne," referring to Robert of Molesme, a co-founder of the Cistercian Order</note>, and later at *Cîteaux* in *Burgundy*; from which they also received the name of *Cistercians* <note>original: "Cisterniensen"</note>, or *Monks of Cîteaux*: and because *St. Bernard* made this order most famous, it is named after him. In *Poland*, the *Franciscan Monks* of the strictest Order are called *Bernardines*. *Miraeus, Book 5, Chapter 4, etc.* <note>original: "Miræus. lib. 5. cap. 4. &c."; referring to the works of the historian Aubert Miraeus.</note>

->**PENITENTS or PENITENTIARIES**<- is the name of certain religious devotees who have formed various brotherhoods, especially in *Italy*, and make it their work to practice public penance at a certain time of the year. It is said that this custom was established in the year 1260 by a *hermit* who preached in the city of *Perugia* <note>original: "Perouse"</note> in *Italy* that the inhabitants would be buried under the ruins of their houses, which would collapse upon them, if they did not appease the wrath of God through immediate penance. Following the example of the *Ninevites* <note>The people of Nineveh who, in the biblical Book of Jonah, repented in sackcloth to avoid divine destruction</note>, his listeners clothed themselves in sackcloth and, armed with rods and whips, made a procession through the streets, striking themselves most severely on the shoulders to do penance for their sins. This type of penance was since practiced in several other countries, and especially in Hungary during a raging *Plague* that devastated that entire kingdom. But a short time later, this gave rise to the formation of a dangerous faction of *Flagellants* (a) <note>original: "Geesselaars"</note>, who ran in entire bands, naked to the waist, covering themselves in blood with violent lashings, and proclaimed that this bloody baptism (for so they called it) washed away all sins, even those they might commit thereafter. (a) The **League** <note>original: "Ligue"</note> was a famous and powerful alliance in the sixteenth century in **France**, and was also called the **Holy Union**; it was first brought to prominence by the **Cardinal of Lorraine**. **CARMELITES**, monks of **Our Lady of Mount Carmel**, who gathered together in the twelfth century on the aforementioned mountain in **Syria**, and in the year 1205 received the Rules of their Order from **Albert**, Patriarch of **Jerusalem**. They subsequently came to **Europe** in the year 1238, where they expanded greatly, and in the year 1568, **Teresa**, a lady of **Avila** in **Spain**, gave the old strict rule of the Carmelites—first to the women and then to the men—to follow, with the approval of **Pope Pius V**. **John of the Cross** <note>Original: "Johannes de Cruce"</note> and **John of Jesus** <note>Original: "Johannis de Jeſu"</note> came to the aid of this reform; both adopted the strict rule of this Order, which was approved by **Pope Clement VIII** in the year 1580. ### Appendix of the CA

**CARTHUSIANS**, a spiritual order among the *Roman Catholics*, take their name from the place *Chartreuse* or *Carthuse* <note>original: "Cartreuse or Carthuse"</note>, three miles from *Grenoble*, in the rugged mountains of *Dauphiné*, in *France*. **CELESTINES** are certain monks whose Order was established by Pope *Celestine V* while he was still a hermit, in the year 1244; approved by *Urban IV* in the year 1264, and confirmed by *Gregory X* <note>original: "Gegrorius X."; likely a typographical error in the source</note> in the year 1274, at the second *Council of Lyon*, to which the aforementioned *Celestine* traveled on foot. This Order expanded greatly in *Italy* in a short time and was introduced to *France* by King *Philip the Fair* <note>original: "Philippus den Schoonen"; Philip IV of France</note>. He commanded his envoy *Petrus de Sorte* in *Naples* to request the General of this Order to send twelve monks of this Order to *France*. When these *Celestines* arrived there in the year 1300, the King gave them two monasteries. Later, in the year 1352, the Dauphin *Charles* <term>Dauphin: the title given to the heir apparent to the French throne</term> brought six more there.

### CENOBITES 
are those monks who reside in monasteries and perform religious services, in contrast to the *Hermits* <note>original: "Kluisenaars"; those who live in isolation</note>.

### CHARITES OF OUR LADY
is a spiritual Order established according to the Rule of *St. Augustine*. It was founded at *Châlons* in *Champagne* by Lord *Guy*, hereditary Lord of *Joinville* and *St. George*. Later, it was confirmed by the Popes *Boniface VIII* and *Clement VI*. *Antonin. Spondan. in Ann. A. C. 1290 n. 1.* <note>Reference to the historical annals of Henri de Sponde</note>

### CHARITES, or BROTHERS OF CHARITY or MERCY, 
<note>original: "Fratres Charitatis vel Misericordiæ"</note> were established by *John of God* in the 14th century to provide assistance to the sick. Popes *Clement VIII* and *Paul IV* confirmed this Order. They follow the Rule of *St. Augustine* and, besides the three standard vows <term>vows: the traditional monastic promises of poverty, chastity, and obedience</term>, they have also taken a fourth: the *care of the sick*. They can never be promoted to any higher status <note>meaning they remain lay brothers rather than becoming priests</note> and beg for their sick with these words: *Give to our poor brothers for God's sake.* For this reason, they are called *Fate bene, fratelli* <note>Italian: "Do good, brothers"</note> in *Italy*. See *Merciful Brothers, p. 409.*

### CHORALISTS and VICARS 
are those who are kept in the collegiate churches <term>collegiate churches: churches managed by a non-monastic community of clergy called canons</term> to sing the Hours <term>Hours: the Liturgy of the Hours, the daily cycle of prayers</term> in the morning and evening in place of the *Canons*, and to observe the *Vespers* <note>Vespers: the sunset evening prayer service</note>.

### CIRCATORES 
were certain *Clergy* in the monasteries who were chosen from among the other brothers to continually visit the cells and keep watch over the monks. If they heard someone laughing or making the slightest noise, they recorded that person’s name, and he subsequently received a reprimand from the *Prior* or *Abbot*. They also had to ring the bell to call the monks together for the hours of prayer and to wake them during the night. Those who visited the monasteries or churches of their Order on behalf of the Superior General were also called *Circatores* <note>Latin: "visitors" or "inspectors"</note>.

### CISTERCIANS, or CISTERCIAN ORDER 
began in the year 1089 and was named after the beautiful Monastery of *Cîteaux* <note>original: "Cisterce"</note>, located in *Burgundy*, four hours from *Dijon*, where there are many *cisterns* <note>The name Cîteaux was historically believed to derive from "cisterna" due to the marshy ground</note>. The first founders and Arch-Abbots at *Cîteaux*—*St. Robert*, *St. Alberic*, and *St. Stephen*, along with several others—had been devout *Benedictines*. Driven by a desire for a stricter observation of the Rule of *St. Benedict*, they departed from the Monastery of *Molesme* <note>original: "Molismus"</note> with the permission of *Hugh*, Archbishop of *Lyon*, and the Papal Legate, into the wilderness of *Cîteaux*, where they began this new Cistercian Reformation,

## Appendix of the Ci[stercians]

so that the Monks of this Order are actually *Benedictines*: yet they were called *White Monks* shortly after their establishment, while the true *Benedictines* were given the name *Black Monks* for the sake of distinction; however, for a long time since, a heavy dispute has arisen among some Roman Catholic scholars—which still remains unresolved <note>original Dutch idiom: "aan den spyker hangt," literally "hangs on the nail"</note>—as to which was the oldest color of the *Benedictine Monks*, the *white* or the *black*. In the year 1113, under *St. Stephen* <note>St. Stephen Harding, one of the three founders of the Cistercians</note>, the third *Cistercian* Abbot, the holy youth *Bernard*, along with thirty other noblemen, joined the Order at the aforementioned place, becoming in the year 1115 the first Abbot of the new Monastery at *Clairvaux* <note>original: "Claraval"</note>. This Monastery is the third direct daughter of the *Cistercian Arch-foundation* <note>Cîteaux, the "Aartssticht" or mother-house from which the order began</note>, and one of the four primary head and mother-monasteries of the entire Order, which are named *La Ferté* <note>original: "Firmitas"</note>, *Pontigny* <note>original: "Pontigniacum"</note>, *Clairvaux* <note>original: "Claravallis"</note>, and *Morimond* <note>original: "Marimundus"</note>, from which the descending lineages are traced to all other Monasteries, which—according to the account of *P. Although *St. Bernard* was not the first founder of the *Cistercian Order*, the Order nevertheless regards him as its *Patriarch* and greatest propagator, because it was greatly extended and increased through him and the numerous and fine Monasteries he established.

# CI Religious Orders.

Some Roman Catholic writers of this Order have strange things to tell concerning the singular favor which the *Holy Virgin* <note>The Virgin Mary, to whom all Cistercian monasteries were traditionally dedicated.</note> has shown to their Order more than once in a miraculous way. Cardinal *Bona* <note>Giovanni Bona (1609–1674), a Cistercian abbot and cardinal known for his writings on liturgy.</note>, who is considered such a wise man among his fellow believers and who belonged to this Order, also recorded such tomfoolery as true histories in his work *On Divine Psalmody, chapter 12* <note>original Latin: "de Divin. Pfalm., cap. 12."</note>. For example, he tells that *the Holy Virgin made a promise of marriage to Robert, the first founder of this Order (as has been mentioned), and gave him a ring as a pledge. Furthermore, she personally handed a white cowl* <note>The "witte Kap," the distinctive white habit of the Cistercians that set them apart from the "Black Monks" of the Benedictines.</note> *to Alberic and Stephen, his successors.* 

St. *Bernard*, that great promoter of this Order, was especially not to be left out of her favors; therefore, she gave him—*what shameless lies!*—her own breasts to suckle <note>This refers to the "Lactation of St. Bernard," a popular medieval legend and artistic motif where the Virgin Mary sprinkles milk from her breast into the saint's mouth or eyes.</note>. Then he relates from the monk *Caesarius* <note>Caesarius of Heisterbach (c. 1180 – c. 1240), a Cistercian monk famous for his collection of miracle stories.</note>, without expressing any disapproval, how a certain monk of this Order saw all the Saints in Heaven during a spiritual ecstasy. *He saw persons of all ranks, and also of all kinds of Orders—that is, to speak only of the Orders, he saw Benedictines, Norbertines* <note>Also known as Premonstratensians.</note>, *Franciscans, and so on. But however much he looked in every direction, he saw no Cistercian monks. While he brooded over this and became disheartened by these thoughts, Our Dear Lady lifted up her cloak—which surely could not have been a short cloak—for under that cloak he saw an uncountable number of Cistercian monks and nuns, sitting huddled together, one on top of the other.* So close did this Order lie to the heart of the *Holy Virgin*.

### CI

The General of this Order is always the Arch-abbot at Cîteaux <note>original Dutch: "Cisterce," the mother house of the Cistercian Order in France</note>, who is named by the Kings of *France* as a born member of the high Royal *Burgundian Tribunal* and is called the first Counselor. 10. The **STRICT REFORMATION OF LA TRAPPE**, begun in *France* not long ago <note>This refers to the Trappists, a reform movement that emphasized extreme austerity, silence, and labor</note>.

1. The **ORDER OF THE TEMPLARS** <note>original Dutch: "Tempelheeren"</note>, who formerly made themselves very famous in the world, as they arose after the conquest of the *Holy Land* around the year 1118. Such riches made them powerful, proud, and hated by everyone due to many failings; for which reason, from the year 1306 to 1311, they were entirely exterminated in a gruesome manner by *Pope Clement V* and *King Philip the Fair* of *France*. Their properties were assigned by the Pope partly to the local lords and partly to the *Order of St. John*—or later the *Knights of Malta*.

[was] founded, and first by **Pope Innocent III** and later by **Pope Honorius III** in the year 1223, confirmed. ### E.

**CONCEPTION**, thus is a certain **Order of Nuns** named, having as its founder **Beatrice de Silva**, born in **Portugal**, and confirmed by **Pope Innocent VIII** at the request of **Queen Isabella of Castile**. In the year 1489, he gave them the **Rules of the Cistercian Order**. ->D.<-

**DOMINICANS**, a famous **Order of Monks**, thus named after **St. Dominic de Guzman**, whose **Rule** <note>The set of spiritual and administrative laws governing the order</note> they adopted in the 13th century. **Johannes Michaelis** reformed them, and **Pope Paul V** confirmed the new arrangement in the year 1608. Their principal work is to apply themselves to **Preaching**, which is why they are also commonly called the **Order of Preachers**. They manage the well-known **Inquisition** in **Spain**, and have had great disputes with the **Franciscans** regarding the **Immaculate Conception** of the **Holy Virgin** <note>The theological debate over whether Mary was born without original sin; the Dominicans traditionally questioned the doctrine while the Franciscans defended it</note>, and with the **Jesuits** regarding the manner of converting the **Chinese** to the **Christian Faith** <note>Refers to the "Chinese Rites controversy," a dispute over whether traditional Chinese ancestor rituals were compatible with Christianity</note>. They go about dressed in white, but when they go out they also put on a black cloak and black hood; there are also **Nuns** of this Order.

Spiritual Orders.

## E.

**ORDER OF HERMITS** of *St. Augustine* is said to have its origin from *William*, Duke of *Guyenne* <note>A historical province in southwest France</note>, a disciple of *Bernard*, who established Hermits according to the Rule of *St. Augustine*. These [hermits] are said to have lived in Monasteries hereafter around the year 1157. Pope *Innocent IV* is said to have assigned them their name in the year 1243, and *Alexander IV* their clothing <note>The specific religious habit or uniform of the order</note> in the year 1255.

**EUDISTS** is the name given to a certain Congregation of Secular Priests <term>Secular Priests: Clergy who do not belong to a specific religious order and live "in the world" rather than in a monastery</term>, which was established by Father *Eudes* <note>Saint Jean Eudes (1601–1680)</note>, a brother of *Mézeray*, the Historian of *France*. Father *Eudes* had been a priest in the Congregation of the *Oratory*, and left it to found his own society. Having established the same at *Caen*, it spread from there through many provinces of *France*, but primarily in *Normandy*, such as at *Rouen*, *Évreux*, and *Coutances*. Their goal was to produce holy and upright Clergy for the Church, and to manage those seminaries <term>Kweekschoolen: Literally "nurseries" or training schools for the priesthood</term> which the Overseers <note>Bishops or high-ranking church officials</note> of the Church wished to entrust to their governance. They called themselves the Congregation of *Jesus* and *Mary*. Father *Eudes* made a special vow of devotion to the *Holy Virgin*.
